speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Hon. Howard C. Green (Aciing Prime
Minister): It gives me great pleasure to announce that His Excellency Habib Bourguiba Sr., President of Tunisia, has accepted the invitation of the government to pay a state visit to Ottawa on May 1 and 2. The President and Madame Bourguiba will be the personal guests of Their Excellencies the Governor General and Madame Vanier at Government house during their stay. Details of the program will be announced as soon as arrangements have been completed.
Hon. members will be aware of the significant role which Tunisia has played in international affairs since achieving independence in 1956. President Bourguiba has headed the government of his country since then, and to him personally must go much of the credit for Tunisia's outstanding international contribution. By his wisdom and understanding he has always exerted a constructive influence not only in matters of direct concern to his country but also in major international issues and particularly those involving the Arab world and Africa. It is at the United Nations that Canada has best been able to observe and appreciate the contribution which this dynamic country has made to international understanding.
Any reference to the international posture of Tunisia and the important part played by President Bourguiba would be incomplete without mention of his continuing contribution to a solution of the problem of Algeria. Not only has his moderating influence been felt in the United Nations on this question, but he has been unstinting in his effort to contribute to an honourable solution of a problem which has been such a deep source of friction between his Arab neighbours in Algeria and France. If, as we all hope, this problem is resolved in the near future, the final settlement will owe much to the dedicated efforts of President Bourguiba.
Yesterday I announced to the house the appointment to Tunisia of Canada's first ambassador, Mr. H. F. Feaver. I mentioned, too, that for more than three years His Excellency Mongi Slim has been ably discharging his function as Tunisian ambassador to Canada. It is with regret that we have now received word of Mr. Slim's impending departure for another and very important assignment, for we have learned to value highly his friendship and effectiveness. With President Bourguiba about to visit this country it is, however, particularly fitting that we should receive the welcome news that Mr. Slim's successor is to be the president's son, His Excellency Habid Bourguiba Jr., who will shortly present his letters of credence to the Governor General. His previous appointments have been as Tunisian ambassador to Italy and France, and I am sure the house will agree that the appointment of the president's son here is a mark of the high esteem in which Canada is held by the Tunisian president and government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As I understand the rule pertaining to amendments introduced to motions for second reading, an amendment to be in order must assert a contrary principle. The form which is always followed in such cases, as I recall it, is "That the said bill be not now read a second time but that-Then follows an assertion of the contrary principle. This is not being done in the present case at all. What we have here in effect is an attempt to say that while the opposition are in favour of one provision of the bill they ask the house to decline to give-they do not say second reading to this bill,-but to decline to give second reading to a bill the provisions of which do not include certain other things.
In my submission the amendment shows no adherence to the rule at all in this respect.
The scope of amendments which may be introduced on second reading is very limited, as you well know, Mr. Speaker. When one clears away the mass of verbiage here there are two things which stand out. The first is an attempt to preserve support for one provision of the bill, and then follows an assertion in very vague terms that the house should not give second reading to a bill which does not make provision for certain other things.
I refer to Beauchesne, citation 201, paragraph 12 where it is stated:
An amendment proposing a direct negative, though it may be covered up by verbiage, is out of order.
I invoke that citation, but I also invoke the clear rule that an amendment is not in order unless it asserts a contrary principle, and I do not find this to be the case in the present proposed amendment. In any event, on examination it will be seen that this is not the type

Income Tax Act
of direct assertion of a contrary principle which is required. The amendment talks about not giving second reading to a bill the provisions of which do not include certain things. That is not the form in which a principle contrary to that set forth in this particular bill, No. C-73, can be put for the purpose of the procedure applicable to amendments on second reading.
The final point I wish to make is that the concluding words of the amendment relating to changes which are said not to be included are not changes which are required in the tax law at all. This is taking the house into an area which under the provisions of the Income Tax Act has been conferred by parliament on the executive branch of government. These come within the regulatory powers conferred on the government by the Income Tax Act.
I refer further to Beauchesne, citation 202, paragraph 15, where it is stated:
An amendment approving part of a motion and disapproving the remainder is out of order.
That is precisely what we have here, an attempt to preserve or approve that part of the motion for second reading which relates to one of the provisions of the bill respecting tuition fees of university students, while expressing disapproval of the remainder of the measure. That clearly comes within the ban set forth in citation 202 on page 170. It thus seems that on any one of several grounds this amendment is clearly out of order.

I should like to say a word on the point of order raised in his habitual manner by the Minister of Finance. May I deal with the hon. gentleman's last observation with regard to paragraph 15 of citation 202 of Beauchesne at page 170. The minister says this amendment is out of order because it approves part of a motion and disapproves the remainder.
The hon. gentleman did not read all the references made by Beauchesne, nor has he referred to the other authorities. As a matter of fact this particular amendment is on all fours with an amendment which was moved in the United Kingdom parliament, and I have reference to it in Mr. Bailey's well known book "British Parliamentary Democracy" at page 90, where the author says:
On the second reading the main principles of the bill are discussed. It is in order to speak about the methods proposed for achieving the objects of the bill or about alternative methods which might be employed. The debate might last only a few hours or it may extend over two or three days. Opposition to the bill may take the form of an amendment to the effect that the bill be read "on this day six months" which would, if passed, kill the bill, or by a reasoned amendment setting out the reasons why the bill should not proceed or showing that the objects of the bill could be achieved in some other way.

It is important to note the particular amendment referred to by Bailey in this context, and I shall read the amendment here moved to show that the amendment introduced by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is on all fours with the motion which was allowed in the United Kingdom parliament. That amendment was a reasoned amendment to the national health service bill of 1946, and it was moved by an opposition member of parliament. It was in the following terms:
I beg to move to leave out from ''that" to the end of the question and to add instead thereof- "this house while wishing to establish a comprehensive health service declines to give a second reading to a bill which prejudices a patient's right to an independent family doctor, which retards the development of the hospital service by destroying local ownership-"
-and so on.
The amendment put forward by my hon. friend is in precisely the same form. This amendment says, in effect, that this house while approving the establishment of special features in connection with tuition fees and in connection with non-resident investment in Canada inter alia, declines to give second reading to a bill the provisions of which do not include any changes in the tax laws to provide for implementing the policy proposed in the supplementary budget so as to assist areas where there has been a substantial degree of unemployment over the years. The Minister of Finance says the amendment is out of order though, as a matter of fact, it is in precisely the form in which an amendment was allowed in connection with the national health service bill in the United Kingdom in 1946. On that score the Minister of Finance has not assisted Your Honour in coming to a conclusion with regard to this all-important matter-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: As so often happens.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The hon. member for Essex East needs some help, though.

In May's sixteenth edition at page 530 that distinguished author deals with the question of reasoned amendment. He says:
It is also competent for a member who desires to place on record any special reasons for not agreeing to the second reading of a bill, to move what is known as a "reasoned amendment". This amendment is to leave out all the words in the main question after the word "that" and to add other words; and the question proposed upon the amendment is, that the words proposed to be left out stand part of the question. A reasoned amendment is placed on the paper in the form of a motion and may fall into one of several categories.

(1) It may be declaratory of some principle adverse to, or differing from, the principles, policy or provisions of the bill-
That is exactly what this amendment does. This amendment complains about the fact that in the bill before the house there are not included amendments not with regard to a minor matter but with regard to a matter that was regarded as important enough to be considered as a declaration of policy in the budget speech of last December, and which is still being discussed in this house as a result of the intransigence, if I may say so, of the Minister of Finance.
We are asking that this bill be strengthened by including in it provisions that are not now included. In response to that the Minister of Finance suggests that the existing law already gives the government the authority which we are seeking to have incorporated in this bill. That is one of the very points of the amendment. We are asking that there be incorporated in the form of a legislative amendment the authority which the governor in council now has in respect of a matter so vital as to warrant inclusion in the budget and which should form part of our statutory law and not be capable of giving authority to the government merely by the exercise of a secret order in council. That is one of the principles involved in this amendment.
The Minister of Finance says this is not a direct amendment, as though that were a very important observation in so far as the validity of this amendment is concerned. It is true that the government has acted in this particular matter under an order in council belatedly passed by the governor in council. Our contention is that the matter is of such importance that it ought to be included in an enactment of this house and that the particular authority authorizing the passing of an order in council is an authority that was never envisaged to cover a matter of this fundamental importance.
For those reasons, Mr. Speaker, I would urge Your Honour, and I do so with confidence, to accept this amendment.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Before the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate speaks I wish to say that he should endeavour to meet the point that this amendment can be brought within the terms of the resolution.

That is what I was seeking to do, Mr. Speaker. Evidently the Minister of Finance has had a lapse of memory, because later on March 2, as Your Honour will find from examining Hansard at page 2609, I got up to address the committee and said:
I should like to address myself to the first few words in this resolution which are:
"Resolved that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Income Tax Act and to provide among other things:"
The whole crux of my remarks was that among the other things that ought to be included in the bill as coming within the scope of the Income Tax Act which was being amended were precisely those things dealt with by this amendment, supported by my hon. friend, which I moved earlier today; that is to say, the inclusion in the bill of specific legislative authority for the kind of double depreciation which the government was seeking to give by order in council under existing legislation. Neither the chairman nor the Minister of Finance nor indeed anyone else took the slightest exception to that observation of mine.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
With respect, Mr. Speaker, that is not true. Will the hon. member look at page 2610 of Hansard, where he will see in the second paragraph that when the hon. member for Essex East attempted to revert to this subject I said "Order", and the deputy chairman made a ruling. He said:
Order. The hon. member was referring to what might be put into the Income Tax Act. That was quite in order. But I think the hon. member is going a little further than he is entitled to go-

Since 1 had the floor, after this usual intervention in the middle of speeches perhaps I might be permitted to proceed. I said no exception was taken to my observations, and no exception was taken to my observations, Your Honour. My observations were the only ones that dealt specifically with the point that the amendment I submitted to the house today deals with, namely whether this amendment can be brought within the scope of the bill. Nothing is more obvious than that. What we are seeking to suggest is that this amendment to the Income Tax Act should amend the act with specific respect to a matter which is now dealt with in the Income Tax Act. Surely the minister would not contend, and I am sure Your Honour would not support the contention, that because there is a provision for doing something one way in an existing act of parliament there cannot be an amendment to that act of parliament and provision made to do it in another way. All we are seeking to suggest here is that we find this bill unacceptable because it does not contain a specific provision to do in another way, which we think would be the better way, what the government is seeking to do though it is a new policy, by means of the use of old and existing legislation. If parliament cannot change existing legislation, and if the opposition cannot put forward alternative views as to what the legislation should be, it seems to me that we would have very little legislative function here whatever. However pleasant that would be to the Minister of Finance it is not a conception of parliament, I am sure, that Your Honour would accept.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I was endeavouring to read the observations of the deputy chairman at page 2610 of Hansard of March 2. May I conclude the reading. He said, referring to the hon. member for Essex East:
But I think the hon. member is going a little further than he is entitled to go in asking what has or has not been done in an order in council.
This is the whole matter of double depreciation which hon. members opposite are seeking to drag into this debate now. If it is in order to amend a motion for second reading by bringing in something which lies outside the scope of the bill for which second reading is being moved, it will be perfectly in order to bring in any subject at all that has any relevance at all to the main statute, in this case the Income Tax Act. That is not the test of relevancy on a motion for second reading of a bill to amend an existing statute. The rule is that the relevancy applies to the terms of the amending bill, not to the main statute, because this present hill deals with

only a few of the many sections of the Income Tax Act. Were this amendment to be in order, then, Mr. Speaker, I think literally hundreds of amendments could be introduced on such a motion just dealing with matters that relate to the main existing statute but have no relevancy whatsoever to the amending bill under consideration.

Sir, since you have allowed the minister to speak twice, perhaps I can reply to his last observation. The effect of the last observation of the minister would be that no amendment could be offered to any bill. In other words we must accept or reject the bill en bloc, and that has certainly not been the practice.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: How ridiculous.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The amendment proposed is an amendment on the motion for second reading of a money bill, a bill preceded by a resolution, which distinguishes this bill and the type of amendment which may be moved from other bills which do not have to be preceded by a resolution, so there is that additional limiting factor to amendments which might not be applicable to other bills before the house for second reading.
It is not safe to apply generally decisions with respect to amendments on the second reading of non-money bills to bills which do require a preliminary resolution. In this instance the resolution does contain some general terms which the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has pointed out. The resolution which was adopted by the house begins:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Income Tax Act and to provide among other things-
Then follow paragraphs numbered 1, 2, 3 and so on, setting out a number of specific items. The only argument that troubles me is the question whether "among other things" opens the door to specific propositions which are not enumerated in the resolution itself- I would be inclined to think not from rules of interpretation-which the reasoned amendment would have to contain; and it is agreed that reasoned amendments on second reading are acceptable.
If this were an acceptable reasoned amendment I would have no doubt about it. The question is whether it is that category of amendment, having regard to the necessity of bringing the reasons within the limitations of the resolution. I think my best judgment- and I agree that these are matters of judgment and might be decided in many instances one way or the other-is that the reason

given here, in so far as it is specific or ascertainable, is not within the terms of the resolution, and therefore could not have been incorporated in the bill in the first instance.
As I try to interpret the reason, which is the latter part of the amendment, I read these words:
That the house declines to give second reading to the bill because it does not include tax laws to assist areas where there is a substantial degree of continued unemployment over the years.
I think the hon. member who introduced the amendment would agree that this is pretty indefinite and vague, but it does assert the contrary principle to some other tax laws relating to assistance to areas where there is substantial unemployment and what he has in mind and what he asserts should be in the bill. The resolution in its terms certainly had no place for tax laws to assist areas where there is a substantial degree of continued unemployment-
Before you give the full judgment would Your Honour hear a word on that specific point?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes.

My word is this. If the amendment contained a reason for not accepting second reading, which would be competent for a member to make as a motion to amend the bill itself in committee, then of course it would not be competent to entertain it on second reading. Your Honour ruled on that very point in one instance on another amendment of mine some years ago, perhaps two sessions ago, when I sought to do by a reasoned amendment something which was competent to do in committee on the bill itself because it was within the scope of the terms of the bill, and for that reason it could not be given as a reason for rejecting the bill as a whole. Therefore I would say that if our reason for seeking to get the house to reject the second reading of this bill was something that could be done to transform the bill in committee, then we would be out of order.
It follows, therefore, that if the reasoned amendment could be made at all it must have as its subject matter something that, though germane to the bill, could not be done in committee on the bill itself. I would not argue for one minute that this can be done in committee on the bill itself. Therefore it seems to me, sir, that that is a consideration that it did not seem to me had been brought out before; and before Your Honour gave a ruling, since this is an important matter, I thought I should draw it to your attention.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I appreciate the force of the argument that an amendment which might

Income Tax Act
be made at the committee stage to a particular section might also be expanded into a reason. If they were the same then presumably the ruling referred to would prevent it being used as a reason, because it could be dealt with in committee. But many reasons could be advanced against reading this bill the second time which would be within the scope of the resolution and yet would not be specific amendments to clauses, and I think I can give an example which will satisfy the hon. member. It would be a reason of principle that the effect of a particular tax measure would be to interfere with trade or investment between two countries, or something of that kind which would not be the subject matter of an amendment in committee. In the result I find that this latter part does not satisfy my mind that it is a reason which can be advanced on this bill because of the preliminary stage.
There is a further difficulty which I think is a real one, in that the amendment seeks to approve part of the bill and to disapprove the remainder. There is fairly clear authority on that point which has already been referred to. As found in Beauchesne, fourth edition, page 170, it is stated:
An amendment approving part of the motion and disapproving the remainder is out of order.
Then an instance is given. In effect this amendment attempts to approve that part of the bill which deals with allowances for tuition fees but to disapprove the bill otherwise, and on that ground I think it would fall. The hon. member has the floor and is free, of course, to continue.

Before Your Honour makes a final ruling may I ask Your Honour to consider the case in the United Kingdom parliament to which I referred, which was a specific amendment following a specific rule. A money bill was involved and the mover of the amendment expressed his approval of parts of the main content of the bill and rejected others for certain reasons. I will admit there is that statement in Beauchesne, but it so happens that in the case of that learned authority there is a mere assertion which, without the citation of instances, surely makes the statement of that learned author nothing more than an authority of persuasive value, whereas in the case I have cited we have a decision of the Speaker of the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
May I say to the hon. member for Essex East that I appreciated the force of his argument and the precedent he produced, and distinguished it in my mind, because the first part of the amendment he cited is simply a general declaration in favour

of a national health policy. It does not really approve part of the bill, and it is quite different from the amendment before us which attempts to approve specifically some provisions of the bill. In the other case there is a general declaration in favour-I do not recall the exact words-of the institution of a national health program, but that is not specific approval of something in the bill itself, and on that ground I distinguish it.

Perhaps I might resume my observations on second reading of the bill itself just long enough to express a regret that the government has not seen fit to take parliament into its confidence and give parliament an opportunity on the bill amending the Income Tax Act to make specific provision for double depreciation for what it pains hon. members so much to call distressed areas. When one thinks of the flights of eloquence that issued from this side of the house over the years from 1940 to 1957 from the present head of the administration, those immediately surrounding him and, not the least, from the Minister of Finance himself about the evils of government by order in council, about the restoration of the rights of parliament, about taking parliament into the government's confidence, about permitting parliament to have a share in the conduct of affairs, it does seem to me that in seeking to inaugurate a new policy of this kind it is a pretty sad thing for the government to follow the procedure of acting by order in council in a matter which they profess is going to be of such very great importance, as this was supposed to be when the advance pre-Christmas billing was given in the baby budget but which has turned out, of course, to be such a damp squib that it is perhaps understandable that the government did not want to make any reference to it in the bill. The government was so ashamed of what a poor, puny little mouse the mountain had laboured and brought forth that it preferred to have that labour in secret and to have the mouse concealed as much as possible, instead of allowing members of parliament the opportunity to discuss the matter and put forward amendments which would not perhaps affect the balance of ways and means but which might make the scheme more effective.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, it does seem to me very unfortunate that this government, which was going to restore the rights of parliament that had been so eroded, to use another of the minister's favourite words, by the previous government, should now be doing something which I cannot ever imagine the previous prime minister or any of the previous ministers of finance attempting to do in this hole in the corner fashion. It is all the more

astonishing when one recalls that the very day before the order in council was passed, whose provisions or better provisions, we think, should be in the bill itself; the very day before when anyone who knows anything about the processes of government knows that the recommendation must have been before the government, must have been in the privy council office in the last stages of being processed, the minister by every possible device of evasion evaded the simple, straightforward questions which the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River was asking-
