speechtext: The hon. member for Welland has proposed an amendment, and I think it would be appropriate to consider it for a moment before he proceeds with his discussion of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
copies of this further amendment have not been furnished us, so I really am not in a position to discuss it in detail or comment on the detailed terms included in it. I have only heard the hon. member for Welland reading it, but it seems to me that it is a repetition, in essence, of the amendment which you have just ruled out of order. It offends the same rules of the house as that previous amendment did, including the citation at page 170 of Beauchesne, that an amendment approving part of a motion and disapproving the remainder is out of order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am inclined to agree. I express my preliminary view that while there is some change in the form of this amendment from the amendment moved by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, I do not see that there is sufficient change to alter the principle which would be applicable to it. If the hon. member for Essex East wishes to speak I will hear him.

I had thought that the case of the amendment proposed in the United Kingdom parliament in 1946 was applicable in every particular to the amendment that was introduced by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. However, Your

Income Tax Act
Honour did point out a flaw when he indicated that in the amendment proposed in 1946 the approval of the bill was in general terms. The amendment now before the house expresses no opposition to the general principles of the bill but finds an inadequacy in the bill, because it does not deal with the specific matter of providing legislatively for authority to deal with the matter of double depreciation. The amendment, therefore, which Your Honour now has before him moved by the hon. member for Welland does meet the objection which Your Honour pointed out, differentiating the amendment of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate from the amendment moved in the British house in 1946.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Would the hon. member allow me to have the text he refers to, and while I am considering it, the hon. member for Welland might continue with his remarks.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Minister of Finance took objection when anyone on this side of the house referred to the exchange rate or the value of the Canadian dollar. He said it had nothing to do with these income tax resolutions. One of the clauses of this bill has to do with the imposition of a 15 per cent tax on interest on bonds held by non-residents. The minister himself, as a reason for this tax, said:
Under current conditions it is not helpful to the balance of payments-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Would the hon. member indicate what page he is reading from?

I am reading from page 1009 of Hansard. The minister is reported as follows:
Under current conditions it is not helpful to the balance of payments, to the exchange rate or, indirectly but more important, to the employment situation, to continue to encourage provincial, municipal or corporate borrowers to issue bonds in other countries.
The minister gave that as a reason for the imposition of this tax; so that our municipalities and provinces would not be going out of the country to such a great degree to borrow money. He admitted that this would increase the inflow of capital from outside and therefore increase the value of our dollar.
I think we should have some opportunity to refer to the exchange rate during the discussion of these income tax resolutions. I agree with the minister in his statement, but I do not agree that he alone and no one else in this house can discuss the exchange rate or the value of the Canadian dollar during the discussion of these income tax resolutions, and that in effect is what he said yesterday.

I suggest that if the minister did not take all the money available in Canada to meet his requirements, our provinces and municipalities would not need to go to New York to borrow money, or not to such a great degree.
The governor of the Bank of Canada said that among the problems that would have to be faced would be that of moderating the rate of capital inflow into Canada. This is what the minister is attempting to do by these income tax resolutions. At page 19 of the Bank of Canada annual report the following statement appears:
The basic reason why interest rates are lower in the United States than in Canada is that the total level of borrowing, the aggregate demand for funds by governments, business and individuals combined, is less (proportionately) in the United States than in Canada.
I maintain that the minister is the worst offender in demanding more money from our economy. According to the minister pension funds are increasing by $300 million a year. Canadian workmen and Canadian people are putting aside $300 million a year into pension funds. All I can say in this regard is that even if the minister had impounded this $300 million each year for the last four years there would not be enough money in these funds to cover his overspending on current account alone. If the minister's money requirements during this next year are anything like the amount prophesied by the Canadian tax foundation, I suggest the provinces and municipalities will have to go to New York to get money to a greater extent than they have heretofore. If they do go to New York for money and there is a tax imposed on the income from the bonds, I maintain that the minister then will be taxing our provinces and the municipalities for their capital expenditures, because in the price of the bond and in the rate of interest the lenders will charge an amount to cover this 15 per cent tax on income from these particular bonds.
In a speech in New York the minister said that these measures were not antagonistic towards United States capital coming into Canada. However, in his budget speech he said that this measure would withdraw some of the special incentives which were designed to attract foreign capital.
I do not see how both these things can be so. In one case it is said the measure is designed to keep out foreign capital, and in the other case the minister says it is not designed to prevent United States capital coming into Canada.
In my view the real reason for the influx of foreign capital is the differential between interest rates in Canada and those in the

United States. I say that the minister himself has contributed to this differential more than any other person in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, there were some other matters with which I intended to deal. There is the question of high interest rates. The minister proposes now to tax bonds that are issued at less than par value. In the past the minister has done this and has thus allowed wealthy people to escape their rightful taxation. Now, when the provinces are doing what he did, the minister says they cannot do it. In the past he has made it possible-
They had to compete with him somehow.
-for corporations with high income tax of 50 per cent or more to net about 5.3 per cent after income tax, or the equivalent of nearly 10.6 per cent before income tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Nonsense.
I think this is absolutely wrong, and again I say the minister should start to clean house at home before he starts after the provinces.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think I should now deal with the proposed amendment. The amendment which has been submitted by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan) is substantially the same as that which was dealt with earlier, the difference being that the first few lines read:
This house, while not opposing all the features of the hill, declines to give second reading-
Whereas the previous amendment read:
This house, while wishing to establish special measures in connection with tuition fees and nonresident investment in Canada, inter alia, declines to give second reading-
I think they are substantially the same. The statement that the house does not oppose all the features of the bill is equivalent to a statement that the house approves some of the features of the bill. As I said before, I do not think the house has accepted amendments which attempt to approve the bill in part at second reading and at the same time disapprove it in part. On that ground alone, I would not accept this proposed amendment.
With regard to my former ruling on the latter part of the amendment, to make clear what I had in mind, I would say that it may be asserted as a reason that the bill does some things that are not acceptable to the house, and that might constitute an acceptable amendment. But what is attempted to be said here is that because the bill does not make tax provisions to assist areas where there is extensive unemployment, the house declines to proceed.
Income Tax Act
Admittedly the bill does not make those provisions, and in my view the bill could not make those provisions without going back to the resolution stage and broadening the resolution to permit such provisions to be introduced into the bill.
That was the point made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), and it seems to me that is an insuperable obstacle to the amendment. Therefore with regret I have to advise the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan) that I do not think his amendment comes within the rule.
I must inform the house that if the hon. minister speaks now he will close the debate.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall be brief. I have no intention of following the practice of some hon. members opposite who have spoken of matters that lie quite outside the scope of the bill. This is not a continuation of the budget debate; it is a debate on second reading of Bill No. C-73.
Yesterday the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) raised a question concerning the lapse of time between the introduction of the bill and the motion for second reading. This bill was introduced on March 2 after the antecedent resolution had been reported out of the committee of ways and means and adopted. We moved for second reading on March 15.
This is not an unusual period of time to elapse between first and second readings of the annual bill to amend the Income Tax Act. Indeed last year when I sought to move second reading, I think one week after the bill had been introduced and given first reading, objection was taken that some of those who are interested, the professional organizations who make a study of the technical features of such bills, had not had enough time to complete their detailed examination.
Therefore there has been no unusual delay in this case. It was a matter of affording the usual period of time for such study as those interested might wish to make of the measure.
The hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) raised a question yesterday concerning tuition fees. I think he may not have fully informed himself of the amendment that was made in the committee of ways and means on the resolution respecting the tax position of students paying university tuition fees and the parents of such dependent students. I think he will find the answer in the terms of the measure itself. However, if the hon. member wishes to raise the matter at the committee stage, I think that would be the appropriate place in which to discuss it.

Income Tax Act
I agree.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will not attempt to review the remarks of some hon. members. The remarks of the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan) this afternoon were thoroughly wild in many respects. He has made these remarks before and persists in making them time and again and I shall not take up further time of the house with denials of these very wild assertions.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Flynn in the Chair.
On clause 1-Obligation issued at discount.
Mr. Chairman, would the minister give the committee an explanation of the purpose and intent of this clause beyond that given in the explanatory notes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think this matter was very fully explained in the budget speech. Its necessity arises from the way in which some provinces in particular, and municipalities have been issuing bonds with a very low coupon rate and issuing them at a substantial discount. I gave some instances in my budget speech on December 20 and the hon. member is, I am sure, aware of them.
The only point which I think could usefully be added to the remarks I made in the budget speech on December 20 and to the explanatory notes in the bill, would concern the position of treasury bills. In the case of treasury bills the lender is remunerated by receiving an amount on redemption which is in excess of the purchase price of the security. This remuneration has been taxed in the past and this practice will continue. However, this income is made subject to tax by a provision already in the Income Tax Act. It is not intended that a purchaser of treasury bills should also be made subject to a further tax under these new subsections added by clause 1.

I think the minister stated that what I said was wild. I referred to the fact that a particular bond sold at a discount returned something over 5 per cent after income tax to corporations having a 50 per cent income tax assessment. I should like to ask the minister whether that is not so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Whether what is not so?
That it would return to corporations paying 50 per cent income tax over 5 per cent after income tax had been paid.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If the hon. member is speaking about a particular case I

shall have to have all the details of the case about which he is asking me.
Yes. I am thinking of that particular 3 per cent bond which was sold at 94.65-I think that is the amount.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As I indicated at an earlier stage, there is only one case since the present government came to office where an issue of bonds by the treasury would have been subject to the tax provided for in clause 1 if it had been in effect.
The minister said my statement was wild. I said the net return would be over 5 per cent after income tax to certain corporations. Is that so or is it not so? Where is my statement wild?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member has made assertions of that kind in the past and I have endeavoured to correct them. He goes on making them. If he wishes a detailed comment on what is the effective interest rate in any particular case perhaps the hon. member would give me particulars of any case he has in mind. I shall then be glad to give him an answer. I have already made my comment on the kind of statements he made in an earlier stage of this debate today. We are dealing now with the question of whether there should be a tax applied with a view to discouraging the practice of issuing these bonds at a discount price with a very low interest rate-
Below a hundred.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Let me explain. This does not apply in the case of any bond where the coupon rate is 5 per cent or more but in the case of bonds issued with a coupon rate below 5 per cent. If the effect is to create a difference of 33J per cent as between the effective yield and the coupon rate, then this clause will apply a tax in the case of the first holder. This, of course, applies only in the case of issues where the issuing authority is not subject to income tax. It will not apply to issues by corporations.

Yesterday I quoted a newspaper report on a debate which occurred in 1959 on this subject of discounts on government bonds and the advantages which accrue under certain circumstances to people in the high income tax bracket. The minister, as usual on technical grounds, challenged me and said I should bring forward the words used in that debate as they are found in Hansard rather than quote from a newspaper, as I did yesterday, the slurs which he had tossed to me then in debate, just as he tossed slurs to the very well informed member for Welland today when he called his statements in connection with these matters "wild as usual".

Normally these matters would not have to be dealt with over and over again. Some of us do not have the argumentative capacity of the Minister of Finance on questions of this kind which really, in effect, results in aspersions upon the integrity and intelligence of those who have the obligation, as part of their democratic duty, to question some of the hon. gentleman's parliamentary activities. If the hon. gentleman's assertions were correct and could be substantiated, a great deal of time and debate would be eliminated because we would have no justification for continuing the argument. But I must refer back to one of the early assertions in this discussion to illustrate what we are being asked to do under this new legislation in order to reduce the opportunities for tax exempt borrowers to issue bonds at a first issue price that is considerably discounted below the eventual price which will be paid when due for repayment.
Under these circumstances, and particularly if the term of the lending is relatively short, there is a provision in our tax laws which results in a capital gain. This is exceedingly important as a bond selling gimmick, and I am using a term which the hon. member for Welland has often, and very properly, used. This gimmick, while not understood too well except to sophisticated lenders, is of extreme importance when it comes to competition among governments seeking funds from the savings of the public. This includes borrowers at federal level, and the Minister of Finance has been the giant in that field in recent years. He competes with others for the savings of Canadians and, indeed, for the savings of investors even outside Canada if he offers a sufficiently big reward for the money he borrows. The hon. gentleman competes with the municipalities and with the provinces for such funds.
Now on March 18, 1959, I referred to this subject just as the hon. member for Welland referred to it and again today. There has just been an attempt made to cut him down with a broadside that his statements were "wild". As reported on page 2027 of Hansard of March 18, 1959, I pointed out that the Minister of Finance was so desperate for funds he was offering special attractions, attractions which were of unusual value to people for whom a capital gain was important in relation to their income tax. Indeed, this attraction had a net result for those whose prevailing income tax rate was at least 50 per cent which was far beyond what the figures inserted by the Minister of Finance in a public advertisement might have led unsophisticated readers to imagine was the cost to the government of this borrowing.
Income Tax Act
I referred also to an other bond advertisement in the name of the Minister of Finance which appeared on February 16, 1959. In great big letters reference is made to one year plus one month bonds at nominally 2f per cent interest. As I say, the unknowing investor, the average citizen, might think, "We have a very competent Minister of Finance and even in these times of relatively high interest rates seemingly he is able to borrow money on our behalf at the rate of 2f per cent". But if we look at the fine print, we see why we have now this clause of the bill. Reference is made to the discount to certain lenders. This is all-important as I pointed out in the debate on March 18, 1959 when, as reported at page 2027 of Hansard, I said:
In the minister's advertisements to the public the issue is referred to as 2% per cent, due April 1, 1960, issued at 97.90, a discount from 100 to yield on that basis 4.76 per cent-
That is ostensibly the effective rate of interest for everybody, not 2| per cent. I went on to say:
I want to point out to the minister that the corporation tax is approximately 50 per cent and that a great number of the personal taxpayers who buy bonds are paying on the last portion of their income an income tax of at least 50 per cent. The result is that people in that category who buy these bonds would have to get a rate of 6.6 per cent on another bond sold at par in order to net the same. That is how attractive the minister has been forced to make his interest rates for his purposes.
Corrective action is being taken in this bill at this time after these things were pointed out to the minister, because the hon. gentleman found that he was not the only one who could play this game. There are other tax exempt borrowers, such as the provinces and the municipalities, and they are beating him at this game of gimmicks. So the minister is now plugging this loophole.
Following the experience of yesterday, I want only to show that the minister's attitude toward ordinary debate here has not changed over the years. Two years ago this was the kind of language used against me when I advanced in this chamber what I thought was an accurate and appropriate argument in debate on this subject. The minister referred to me, as reported at page 2027 of Hansard of March 18, 1959, in the following terms:
Surely my hon, friend is not going to leave on the record a shockingly misleading and inaccurate statement of that kind.
The minister's well known adjectives.

As the hon. member for Essex East says, these are adjectives which come from the mouth of the minister so

Income Tax Act
frequently that we cannot, after constant repetition, believe that they appropriately apply time after time.
I could deal with another similar short term issue of June 15, 1959 but it is not my wish to burden the committee members. However, as I said yesterday, in June 1959 there was also given an effective interest rate to a lender in a 50 per cent income tax bracket over a term of about 13 months only which would have required, if the bonds had been issued at par and at a fully stated rate of interest, a real interest rate in excess of 8 per cent. I see it was 8.27 per cent. That is what taxpayers of this country paid for money at that time.
When this was brought to the attention of the citizens of our country as we felt it our duty to do the minister tried to mow us down saying that we made misleading, malicious and inaccurate statements.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think I ever said malicious.
That is a word very commonly used by the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. It is a Liberal word, an Essex East word.
I would be the first to acknowledge that I have tremendous respect for the mental capacity of the Minister of Finance.

Though not for his
judgment.

Indeed, sometimes not for his judgment as for example when he bought money at rates much beyond the rates which private corporations were paying for money at that time, but I suppose the lenders thought it was dandy.
As I said, I should be the first to acknowledge the industry and fundamental intelligence of the Minister of Finance.
And his stubbornness.

But one of the features of that debate that surprised me most was when the Minister of Finance told the hon. member for Welland that he was indulging in wild statements; that he did not know what he was talking about and suggested that, in so far as the length of the term of the loan was concerned, it was an insignificant matter. The debate in this connection occurred on March 18, 1959.
In the course of his remarks on that occasion the minister suggested that selling bonds at a discount was not an unusual practice and that it had been engaged in by the previous administration. The minister gave a number of examples. However, the amazing thing was
[Mr. Benidickson.)
that due to lack of experience in these matters or for some other reason, the minister neglected to place importance upon the length of the term of each borrowing. I think the discount figures recited were 98.5, 99.5, 97 and 99 and in each case he used as illustrations terms that were related to longer issues with the result that, to a lender in a high income tax group it was only insignificant with respect to capital gains.
We have before us in clause 1 an attempt on the part of the minister to stop this form of competition in so far as other non-taxable governmental borrowers are concerned-the provinces and municipalities. I do not in any way object to the purposes of this clause. In fact, I suggested in 1959 that a dangerous trend had been established and I felt that the minister was making opportunities available to lenders that were affecting the people who pay the shot, the taxpayers. As I say, generally most taxpayers in this area are not sophisticated and failed to realize the true cost of the minister's borrowings. I welcome this clause because I realize the trend referred to could reach ridiculous extremes.
The minister did not refer to some of his own borrowings at terrific cost to the treasury. I allude to the cost to the treasury because normally the treasury would receive more income tax from certain lenders. However, if they could avoid the payment of the tax on the capital gains portion of their lending to the government over short periods like 13 months, then the treasury, of course, would suffer a loss. Because of these comments I felt duty bound to reply to the minister's statement of yesterday when he was just as disparaging-I quoted from the newspaper rather than Hansard-of the possibility that I might in some way be accurate. I wish to draw this to the attention of the committee and reassert that events have proven that the warnings which were given by me in 1959 as to the dangers of competition in this field of discounting bonds, and they were also given by the hon. member for Welland, have proven to be well founded. Indeed, the minister himself has come forward now and made sure that there will be limitations on the power of his competitors in the borrowing field, the provinces and municipalities, to do what he did in a most extravagant way since he assumed office as Minister of Finance.

The minister asked me to give him one definite bond. He said I was wild in my reference to the fact that over 5 per cent would accrue to those people paying 50 per cent income tax. He said my statement that this amount would accrue to them after they had paid their income tax was wild.

On October 1, 1959, the minister advertised bonds at 3 per cent. He sold them at $94.65, to mature in 19 months. Afterwards, on the orders of the day, he said that $125 million worth of those bonds were sold. I would challenge the minister to say that the return is not over 5 per cent net to those corporations that paid 50 per cent income tax. He asked me to name one specific bond, and I am naming it.
While the minister is contemplating a reply to that question-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Over 5 per cent? But the hon. member was talking earlier this afternoon about 10 per cent, not 5 per cent. He used this extravagant expression this afternoon.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, when speaking earlier this afternoon, referred to what I said in this house on March 18, 1959. He told only part of the story because it will be recalled that when I was enumerating a list of issues by the former government at discounts, the hon. member for Ottawa West rose and said "Those are not short term". Then, I was able to give him another list of issues by the former government that were precisely of that nature, issues at a discount and with precisely the same effect that he was contending the issues of the present government were having at that time. The fact is-I repeat it, Mr. Chairman-that there has been only one issue in the past three years and nine months by the federal government that would have come within the scope of this present amendment had it been in effect at the time.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has again used very positive and assertive language. He said that I questioned the length of the term and on March 18, 1959, in reply to me, he said that length of bond terms were "precisely" the same under the former government. I will allow the minister considerable leeway over his usual extreme language. In this context he uses the word "precisely". I will send him over my copy of Hansard debates of March 18, 1959. I indicated that the previous government had issued bonds at times at a discount as is the common practice. But I say, the minister used the word "precisely". Will he indicate to me where any of those issues of the previous government were on a basis of anything near a 13 months term?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have sent for the volume of Hansard. I think the hon. member is aware that I have not the volume with me.

No; but I Dromised to send over mine.
Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps the date may not be the same, but I was referring to the time two years ago when we had a two-day debate on a supply motion and this subject was discussed at some considerable length. I gave two extended lists of issues at discounts by the former government.

I agree with the hon. member's recollection of his presentation during a supply motion in 1959 of certain details respecting a lengthy list of issues of government bonds at less than par. My recollection is that on that occasion the minister recited the rate of interest and the issue price. On that occasion I was astonished that after two years in office, in answer to a question raised by the hon. member for Welland, the minister suggested that the question of the length of term of each lending was unimportant.

The minister seems to accept my contention that 5 per cent after income tax is correct. This is one of the statements which he said was wild. He said that I referred to 10 per cent. I did not say that the government was paying 10 per cent. I said these people would receive from the minister the same amount as they would from a bond that paid 10 per cent if sold at par.

Just for the record, Mr. Chairman, because the minister has referred to it again today, at the resolution stage of the Income Tax Act amendments this year, the minister said as reported at page 2614 of Hansard:
-out of all the federal bond issues in the last three years and eight months there is only one to which this resolution would have applied.
I have referred to two issues in 1959; one, I think, in June and one in March or April. Does the minister refer to either of those issues?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My statement
was one made after a detailed study prior to the supplementary budget of December 20 of all the issues of the present government.
The minister does not recall the particular issue to which he referred on Hansard page 2614?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The date, no; I have not the list here at the present time.
It is public information. I will not press the minister for it here.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Clause agreed to.
On clause 2-Tuition fees of students.

Will the minister indicate in what particular I seem to have been misinformed? My point was, briefly,

Income Tax Act
that the bill as it now reads provides tor assistance for the year 1961 only. I had suggested that since the academic year began in the fall of 1960, the provision of benefits should run from that time. The minister seems to suggest that I had not properly understood what the amendment offers, and I should be very happy to be shown where I was wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman. Subclause (2) of clause 2 makes it quite clear that the proposed new subsection (1) of section 11 as amended is applicable to the 1961 and subsequent taxation years. When this matter was discussed on an earlier occasion the question was raised as to payments made by university students in the fall of 1960 of their fees for the 1960-61 academic year. As the resolution appeared in its original form such payments would not have qualified for the intended benefits, but the amendment does open the way now to a student who did pay his 1960-61 academic year fees in September, 1960, let us say, to deduct in his 1961 taxation year that portion of the fees which was paid in respect of the period commencing January 1, 1961.
Where does this clause say that? It is clearly stated that the clause is applicable to 1961 and subsequent taxation years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member must look further in the clause. In line 28 he will find the words, "in respect of a period not exceeding 12 months commencing in the year . . ."

Certainly if the minister intends this to apply to 1960 that is very acceptable but I am simply pointing out that the clause does not say that. It is true that in line 28 it says, "in respect of a period not exceeding 12 months commencing in the year", but surely that is qualified by subclause 2 which says that this clause is applicable to the 1961 and subsequent taxation years.
When the bill is passed and some student will go and apply for relief, he will point out what the minister may have said in the house. The tax collector, as will the courts, will not interpret this clause on the basis of the language used by the minister in the house but on the basis of the literal meaning of the words as they appear in the clause. The clause as it is now drawn does not warrant the conclusion which the minister has reached. The only way that can be done is to say that the clause is applicable to 1960-61 and subsequent taxation years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has not been following me today 
with his usual clarity of thought. My remarks are consonant with the provisions of the bill. There will be no difference found between them and the plain language of the bill. The bill does not provide tax relief in respect of the calendar year 1960, but it does offer tax relief for periods commencing January 1, 1961.
That is it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: However, in relation to payments that were made in 1960 in respect of fees for a period commencing on or after January 1, 1961, the amendment introduced in committee of ways and means permits a student to have the benefit of deduction in respect of fees paid in relation to periods following January 1, 1961, notwithstanding that the fees may have been paid prior to that date.

Mr. Chairman, I want to assure the minister that I am speaking without any belligerence. However, I should like him to indicate to the extent he can, the consideration he may have given in preparing his budget proposals to alternatives so far as the actual mechanics are concerned. I think we all approve of the further step he has taken which goes beyond what was initiated by the previous administration to try to provide additional tax exemptions to assist parents and also to encourage students to remain at college.
The federal government cannot enter the field of education directly but this has seemed to be an area in which the federal government can make some contribution by way of encouragement along these lines. I have no doubt that the minister and his officials have given consideration to alternatives. However, I was greatly impressed in reading last month an editorial in an issue of a magazine or newspaper called "Labour" which is distributed to all railroad workers in the United States and also to the members of the international railway brotherhoods in Canada. The editorial comments upon proposals similar to those of the minister today which were advanced in the United States congress. It gives an example which I put before the minister because he will recognize its practical value and the fact that it can be applied to the Canadian situation. The editorial goes on to point out that there are flaws in connection with proposals for tax relief for students in college and has this to say in part:
A $1,500 deduction would save $300 taxes for a family in the 20 per cent income tax bracket. The higher a family's income, the more taxes it would save by the deduction, up to $1,305 saving for a family in the 91 per cent tax bracket.

Here is the point that I think has significance for all of us if we are concerned about making sure that those who need help most are likely to be helped through the mechanism of income tax at the federal level where other opportunities to assist are limited. We do make grants to universities, and the desirability of doing this has been challenged somewhat in some quarters from the point of view of whether or not it was an encroachment on provincial rights. We all have knowledge of this argument. If the federal field is limited, are we looking after those whose need is greatest?
The editorial goes on to say that if, instead of a tax deduction, a credit of $500 a year were offered or any other fixed sum as a deduction from the tax of the parent or the student this would be much more consequential so far as actual value to the neediest is concerned. One realizes, of course, that while the provision before us would be of some value to the students it could be of no possible value to the parent in a family whose numbers were sufficiently large and where the over-all earnings were so modest that after deductions the parent either would have to pay no taxes at all or would not pay income tax at an important percentage rate. Therefore the relief to such a parent, who might need help most, would not be too important under the proposal before us compared with some form of fixed lump sum deduction.
I am sure the minister has given consideration to these matters and perhaps he could indicate to us what the difficulties are. It is quite obvious that the parent with a very large income really does not need to be encouraged financially to send his children to college. Under this legislation he gets the benefit of a much larger dollar value in respect of tuition fees and other deductible expenses than the man who is not paying any taxes at all or is paying taxes at such a low rate that 13 or 14 per cent of $1,500 is not nearly as important as 75 per cent or more on the same amount of tuition fee expenditure to a wealthy person.
I wondered if the minister proposed to reply.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
To be brief I would say that any amendment of this kind of course does not apply to all taxpayers but only to those who qualify within its provisions. This provision is intended to provide tax relief to the student who would otherwise be taxable, and will permit him to deduct the tuition fees which he pays from his income in determining whether he is taxable or not. In the case of a parent of a dependent student it means that the amount 90205-6-193
Income Tax Act
of the tuition fees paid will be taken into account in determining whether the student is still a dependent, that is to say, whether he has an income in excess of $950 or not. If, after deducting the tuition fees, the amount of income is below $950 then that student still qualifies as a dependent under the provisions of the act, and the parent in that case is entitled to the full $500 exemption provided. I think the situation is quite clear, Mr. Chairman.

I regret that it is not clear to me and it may be my fault. The minister has been looking over at me with some amusement and on that account I feel very humble in raising the matter again because it may be in this particular instance that I am more obtuse than I normally am. In any event, because there is an important principle involved here, I venture to raise it again.
The minister may have provided for this in some other way but he has not convinced me that he has any authority for the conclusion that he has reached. I have looked around this chamber and asked at least two others whose mental I.Q. I am sure approximates that of the Minister of Finance, even if my own might fall far short, and their conclusion is the same as mine that this measure deals not with the taxpayer who may have dependents but deals rather with the taxpayer who himself is a student. The question I have raised is simply this; this measure provides, with respect to fees paid by students beginning in January, 1961 for a period of 12 months, a relief to that student. My complaint was with regard to those fees paid by the taxpayer student for the full academic term and this measure, as now drawn, does not warrant the conclusion which the minister has given.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I suggest you have misinterpreted the conclusion. I will say this again as simply as I can; there is no change created by this amendment with respect to the 1960 taxation year. The change that was made in the original resolution made it possible for the student who in 1960 paid his tuition fees in full for the academic year 1960-61, to have the benefit of a deduction in respect of those fees applicable to the portion of the academic year commencing January 1, 1961.
I am glad the minister now agrees with me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is all I have said.

The original proposal I made was, why did the minister not

Income Tax Act
extend this provision for the full academic year beginning in the fall of 1960?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, the reason-

May I finish. I am now glad to see that the difficulty of comprehension did not reside with the member for Essex East, but perhaps because of the confusion and all the concerns and preoccupations of the Minister of Finance, it was he who had not understood what apparently all of us now admit is a very simple point; and that is that tuition fees paid in the academic year 1960 should be embraced by this measure. I will tell the minister that I have had a considerable number of representations made to me by students, most of them attending the university in my own city and many of them married. The suggestion I make if adopted would provide them with some assistance, that is, if this measure applied to fees that they either have paid or that are owing for the full term. Some of the students will graduate in May and consequently the provision "not exceeding 12 months" will give them no relief whatsoever. It applies only to those students who will be at the university from January, 1961 until December, 1961. Many of the students will graduate this year and the plea that 1 am making to the minister is that, while this is a good provision-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Thank you.

-and will assist during this period of the emergency of unemployment, many students-I am glad to see that the Minister of Labour applauds this today. This, in an indirect way, provides small relief to many people who are very seriously affected by unemployment. Why does the minister not extend this benefit to the period of the full term so that those who are taxpayers, many of them married, and attending university, can get this relief?
The government has embarked upon a delayed program of vocational guidance, delayed by the Minister of Labour's procrastination, and finally he has accepted our recommendations over the years-

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: You never had any recommendations.
My hon. friend says we never have had any. We have made these recommendations to the Minister of Labour repeatedly while he sat in his seat ignoring this question of unemployment.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Quit laughing when you say that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. May I suggest that the exchange between the hon. member for Essex East and the Minister of Labour is not in order.

I think you are right. I was simply going to say that if the Minister of Labour had the equanimity and the serenity of the Minister of Finance he would not provoke these outbursts.
I appeal to the Minister of Finance, now that he and I do understand this question, to extend the benefits of this provision for the full term so that the 12 months covered in line 28 would run from September or early October to the end of the academic year in the spring of 1961. If the minister would do that he would win, I am sure, the undying affection of thousands of students who find it difficult to follow him now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am glad that the hon. member now understands the effect of that clause. He attributed some element of misunderstanding to me and I hope I have not added to his confusion because that is the last thing I would wish to do. I thought the only thing I did not understand in this situation was the mental process that led him into such confusion in regard to the clear provisions of the clause. I have known the day when he was much clearer in following these explanations of the terms of these clauses than perhaps he has been today.
Let me now deal with the point in substance that he has raised. With respect to any tax change there must be a starting date. In this particular case the budget was introduced on December 20, 1960 and therefore the logical starting date was January 1, 1961. We are dealing with tax years and it is the calendar year that is the taxation year. It is not the academic year; it is the taxation year.
The hon. member has now taken note of the fact that fees paid in 1960 in respect of the academic period commencing January 1, 1961, can be deducted.
Yes, I am clear on that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As to students who were in attendance in 1960 and paid their fees in the autumn of that year, if those students continue in attendance throughout the calendar year 1961 they will of course qualify for the academic fees they have paid for the full year 1961; that is to say, the two portions, the portion paid in respect to the term from January to May in the one academic year and the second portion from September to December in the following academic year.
With respect to those students who will be graduating in the spring of 1961, obviously they will qualify under this clause only for

that portion of the fees paid for the 1960-61 academic year in respect of the period commencing January 1, 1961.
There must be a starting date and that is the reason why the particular date is chosen. Obviously the proper date to choose here was January 1, 1961, which was then within 12 days of the date of the budget and marked the beginning of the new taxation year.

Mr. Chairman, before the minister rose I intended to rise very briefly in support of what I thought was a very eloquent and earnest plea by the hon. member for Essex East. I listened carefully to the minister's explanation. We all understand that there is a calendar year and there must be a starting date. However, I think this is a somewhat different circumstance than applies to most taxation fields. I think the hon. member for Essex East was quite sound when he pointed out that those students who graduate in May this year will only enjoy partial benefit under this measure.
These young people will be going out into the world to seek employment, and so on-
And these students are themselves taxpayers.

Yes, Mr. Chairman, that is a very good point and I am glad the hon. member for Essex East has mentioned it. I do ask the minister to reconsider his decision in this respect. I think that under these circumstances, when we are considering giving some relief to these students, this amendment is very necessary and very worth while. The members of this group are very pleased to see this clause in the bill, but I would earnestly ask the minister to permit an amendment to the clause to provide for the inclusion of fees that are not included at the present time. I refer to fees incurred from last September to the end of the year.
I fully appreciate the minister's argument about the starting date, the calendar year and so on. If I recollect correctly, we have not previously had a situation of this kind in any discussion on the Income Tax Act. These are special circumstances that surround this request for an amendment to the clause.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
when you begin to go back on new legislation you have the same problem of drawing the line. What we are asked to do now is move the date back to September, 1960. What about those students who graduated in the spring of 1960 and paid fees in respect of the term in 1960 from January until May? If they were left out, they would have the same reason to complain.
You can go back further. Those students who graduated the previous year could make 90205-6-193J
Income Tax Act
out the same case. It becomes necessary, under these circumstances, to draw the line. There will always be some people who will be included and some who will be excluded in new legislation of this kind. That will apply no matter what date we choose. There will always be those who made their payments in an earlier period. That is inescapable in legislation of this kind.

I am sure the minister would have the support of the whole opposition if he accepted this amendment. We recognize the validity of his argument in this respect, but I think he would have the support of the whole opposition if he would accept the amendment on that basis, because it is a reasonable request.
You cannot go back year after year, but when you are considering the student year, I agree with the argument of the hon. member for Essex East that the measure should be amended in this way.

Mr. Chairman, I am so encouraged by the support of the hon. member for Kootenay West that I think there may still be some hope of impressing the Minister of Finance.
I agree with the minister that there has to be a starting date, but surely the proper starting date is not the middle of the academic year but the beginning of the academic year. The beginning of the academic year is in the fall. The minister has made this measure start in the middle of the year. I am sure that if this amendment were accepted the loss of revenue to the crown would not be very great.
Clause 2 provides for this kind of relief extending for 12 months in the year. Subclause 2 provides that this clause is applicable to the 1961 and subsequent taxation years-it is going to extend for many taxation years-and time being what it is, surely it would not be a matter of inconvenience to the crown for the measure to begin at the proper time. As I have said, the proper time is not the middle of the academic year but the beginning of the academic year.
We are not asking for a privilege to be afforded to a select group in the country. University education in Canada today is not being pursued as it was in the days of the Minister of Finance and myself, on a somewhat restricted basis. In our universities today we have men who are attending university and working at the same time. Many students are married. The students who came to see me were men who were earning their way by working in one of the Windsor plants. Some of them were married.
It is a very difficult assignment for this type of student to obtain an education under these

Income Tax Act
circumstances. I know the particular financial situation of people like that. The hon. member for Kootenay West, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River and myself are making a plea for a very substantial number of people. We hope that the minister will be consistent and will apply this measure, as he said, at the proper period. The proper period is surely not the middle of the academic year but the beginning of the academic year. If the minister would do that I am sure he would be giving needed assistance to a large body of students in this country, particularly at a time when we are trying to encourage men to become trained in order to maintain our standard of living and to raise it still higher. This is all part and parcel of the process of trying to meet unemployment and the like. This does not seem to be an unreasonable request.
Once again 1 appeal to the minister, who knows the value of this kind of training, who received it himself in circumstances that indicated his own capacity for acquiring an education in the face of difficulties. I ask the minister to remember his student days, the days when he walked across the campus of the University of Toronto with holes in his pants and his stockings. I ask him to remember his own example, and I hope this will be the means by which he accepts the strong plea made by those on this side of the chamber.
This is the kind of occasion when the minister should swallow his pride. He should not be afraid to admit that he has made a mistake. This is the kind of admission that would endear the hon. gentleman to the hon. member for Essex East.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am sure that nothing the Minister of Finance could possibly do could have the effect of endearing him to the hon. member for Essex East more than is the case at this present time.
I do like you.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not recall the holes that the hon. member speaks about. 1 think I was decently, if modestly, attired in those days.
You could not see from behind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have given the reasons in this matter. I can add to those reasons only that after the resolution was introduced on December 20 there were representations from various student bodies and from some hon. members of this house. I recall, for instance, what was said by the hon. member for Regina, and others. The burden of these representations in this

respect was that we should permit the inclusion in the benefit of the clause of payments made by some students in 1960 in respect of that portion of the academic year 1960-61 commencing after January 1, 1961. That was the burden of the representations we received from the student bodies, and effect was given to those representations in the amendment which I introduced into the resolution in the committee of ways and means. It is now reflected in this clause.
I am glad that the merits of this new proposal are so widely recognized that hon. members who have not even raised the question in the past, now think so well of the idea that they would like to see it extended backwards.

I should like to ask the minister a question. Supposing a student starts attending college this coming fall, in September, and has paid his fee, say, $400. Will he be able to charge that $400 against income tax in 1961 or must it be allocated over the number of months he goes to college?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In such a case the student could take the full benefit in the year 1961 or he could take part of it in 1962 if the payment was made in respect of the academic year 1961-62. But he could not have it twice.

I wish to suggest to the minister that he might be able to find an easy way around this difficulty. There is already precedent in the Income Tax Act. I refer to the language which relates to medical expense deductions. There is not a direct tie-up between expenses incurred in the taxpaying calendar year such as the minister suggests is generally necessary. It is stated there that the reduction for medical expenses shall be within the period of 12 months ended in the tax year and not included in the calculation of a deduction for medical expenses for a previous year.
We all know that normally the academic year in this country does not coincide with the calendar year. I am confident the minister will have to make a change to take cognizance of this fact in the future and I suggest that we should let this section stand until we have dealt with the remainder. I should like the minister to consider whether or not he ought to look further at the possibilities in the light of this precedent relating to deductions in respect of medical expenses which, though they confine the deduction to expenditures incurred in a 12-month period they do not necessarily relate to the actual 12 months of the calendar year for which a person has filed an income tax statement.

I think the agile mind of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River has helped the committee to arrive at a solution to this difficulty. I may say that the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, the hon. member for Essex East and the hon. member for Kootenay West seem to be three hearts that beat as one on this issue. I think this is a very worth-while suggestion. I think the argument raised by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River is a valid one and 1 should like to hear the minister's counter argument. I do not see why the minister should be unable to take action along the lines suggested.

I thank the hon. member for Kootenay West for his compliment, though I do not think my mind is as agile as it should have been on this point. I recall now another precedent which I think might be helpful, where deductions are not related to the calendar year. I am thinking of the deduction which is made possible for selfemployed persons in connection with savings plans for the period after their retirement, plans made on a basis resembling payments into a pension fund. My recollection is that such self-employed persons are able to make those contributions without strict restriction to the calendar year. I believe they had an additional leeway of two months-the months of January and February in the year following the calendar tax year-in which to make that contribution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The point raised by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River does not at all touch the problem which has been raised. The point he is raising is really in support of the answer I gave the hon. member for Welland, who asked about the applications of payments made once the clause comes into effect. I pointed out that this new clause extends to a student the benefit of being able to divide the payment between the calendar years embraced in part within the academic year.
This does not touch at all the question of the starting date. There still has to be a starting date and whatever date is chosen we shall find some qualifying after that date and others excluded, just before that date. That is inseparable from the legislation of this kind. We have to fix a date, and we have made the date conform with the first day of this present calendar year. That was a sound and proper date having regard to the date of the introduction of the budget, and the change we have made in this clause in favour of students in the academic year 1960-61 is made in full harmony with the representations addressed to us by the student bodies of this country.

We have heard a suggestion from the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River which I hope the Minister of Finance will accept, namely, to allow this clause to stand so that we may make some progress with the rest of the measure before us. If, after reflection, he is still of the same mind he could tell us so but I would suggest that this clause should stand at the moment in order that we could make some progress.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should very much like to see the committee make some progress, although I cannot accept the suggestion which has just been made. The fact that the minister does not agree is no reason for believing that there may not be others in the cabinet who would take the position put forward from this side of the chamber, and if I judge correctly the temper of this committee there are very few members supporting the minister today who do not share strongly the views which we have put forward on this question this afternoon.

I wish to support the proposal made by the hon. member for Essex East. When he referred to the silent sympathy with his arguments felt by members supporting the government I looked to my left and happened to see the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi. If I read that hon. member's countenance aright he has been very sympathetic to the arguments used by the hon. member for Essex East. Perhaps if we defer consideration of this clause there may be enough young Conservatives down at the Progressive Conservative organization who will express

Income Tax Act
their views and bring this matter further to the attention of the minister and his colleagues. I think the suggestion is a good one. By delay, we might make some further progress.

The hon. member brought up my name in this debate. Let me say that I heartily concur in what the Minister of Finance said. I only hope we can make speedy progress and pass this legislation which is for the benefit of all Canadian students. I see no reason for there being any delay.

-will extend the benefit of the low rate of tax to an additional 4,000 companies. Out of approximately 62,000 corporate income tax payers 55,000 have incomes below $35,000, and will in future pay no more than 21 per cent.

form of which I was more familiar three or four years ago? Is there still a publication of this kind made available by the Department of National Revenue?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:

Income Tax Act

For the record, in reference to this particular clause, I am simply going to give the committee the benefit of expert comment in connection with it. I refer again to the Price Waterhouse statement in the Canadian Tax Journal. So far as I am concerned I am hoping we can conclude our discussion by six o'clock and if the minister will be patient I think we can do it. The statement reads:
On the other hand, the changes in the rules relating to associated companies made earlier in 1960 will limit this benefit to a smaller number of taxpayers than previously enjoyed the lower rate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of course, the reasons for the 1960 amendment were clearly understood at that time. The legislation that had existed up to 1960 had evidently attracted a proliferation of those associated companies, each seeking to qualify for the low rate of tax. And, for reasons which commended themselves to parliament, the amendment of 1960 was introduced and adopted. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Mr. Chairman, I have furnished copies of this amendment today to hon. members of the opposition parties. It is an amendment relating to the sale of treasury bills. There is one change in the text of the proposed clause compared with the copy I gave the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. In the second line of the proposed subclause 3(a) he has the date "March 15, 1961" in his copy. It should be today, of course, and accordingly in the amendment which has been handed to the chairman it is March 16,	1961. Unless the chairman
wishes to read the amendment first, I should like to say a word by way of explanation. The amendment is very long and perhaps it is not necessary to read it. The explanation is to this effect.
This amendment, which adds a new subsection to section 108 of the act, is necessary to facilitate the collection of the non-resident withholding tax on interest in the case of treasury bills sold to non-residents.
Treasury bills are generally sold without a provision to pay interest in the usual way. Instead, the lender is remunerated by receiving an amount on redemption which is in excess of the purchase price of the security.

Income Tax Act
This remuneration is in lieu of interest and should be taxed as interest. It has always been taxed when received by a resident of Canada but before December 20, 1960, it was not taxed when received by a non-resident because the non-resident withholding tax did not apply to interest paid on government of Canada securities.
This amendment provides that when a resident of Canada sells a treasury bill to a non-resident the non-resident shall be deemed to have received a payment of interest. The amount of interest he shall be deemed to have received shall be equal to the proportion of the difference between the original issue price and the face value of the bill, that is, the proportion of the original discount, which is attributable to the unexpired portion of the term of the bill remaining at the time it is purchased by the non-resident.
Since this amendment deems interest to have been paid to the non-resident at the time the non-resident purchased a treasury bill the Canadian resident who sells the treasury bill will be obliged to withhold the 15 per cent non-resident withholding tax on the amount that is deemed to be interest.
If at some subsequent time before maturity the non-resident sells the treasury bill back to a Canadian resident the non-resident will be eligible for a refund of that part of the tax he has paid which is attributable to the unexpired portion of the term of the bill.
In other words, in this case the interest deemed to have been earned is prorated in respect of the period that the bill is held by these several holders.

I cannot recall the definitions as contained in the act but when the minister refers to a Canadian resident does that mean, so far as treasury bills are concerned, a government, in other words, a nontaxpaying borrower via treasury bills?
