AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Chairman,
in speaking on the estimates for the Department of Agriculture I should first of all like to take this opportunity to congratulate the minister on his new portfolio. I am sure he will continue the good work which he carried out in his former portfolio, with which I was closely connected as a result of my interest in national parks.
I am sure that agriculture all across Canada will receive the proper and deserved attention of the new minister. He has already made some notable strides in the department. We in Alberta particularly have witnessed the massive sales of grain which are going to be of direct benefit to the farmers in our province, for which we thank him. We thank the minister and the former minister of trade and commerce for their initiative and ability in getting out and selling our grain.
At this time I wish to touch briefly on some of the major points in our national agricultural policy. I want to mention our crop 90205-6-194i
Supply-Agriculture
insurance scheme. We in western Canada have heard some opposition to this scheme, but we have not heard anything objective.
I should like to suggest through you, sir, that some of the M.L.A.'s in the Alberta legislature would be better off to start considering a crop insurance scheme, rather than making speeches condemning the government for this, that and the other thing. We have initiated a crop insurance scheme which will be of benefit particularly to the farmers in my area. I hope the Alberta legislature will give serious consideration to implementing such a scheme in our province.
Then, I want to talk about farm credit. Certainly no other government has done as much as this one for farm management and the improvement and establishment of economic units in western Canada. My friends in the Liberal party talk glibly about some of the agricultural problems in western Canada. Their glibness is notable for its absolute lack of policy with regard to western agriculture.
I should like to say to the minister through you, Mr. Chairman, that we must be always on the look out to make sure the farm credit corporation does not become stereotyped in its form of loan because, in western Canada and in my area particularly, we have a variety of soils and a variety of farming operations that are suited to the area. I should not like to think that because certain areas in my constituency cannot raise one thing but can raise another they will be hampered in securing from the Farm Credit Corporation proper loans to go ahead and develop a particular kind of agriculture.
Then I would move on to the stabilization act. I think that was a great stride forward, even though the hon. member for Assiniboia did not agree. However, the new program for hogs and eggs has worked out well. As with any new program, some wrinkles will need to be ironed out. The farmers in my constituency feel very strongly that we should give consideration to at least semi-annual deficiency payments on hogs and payment on a regional basis. We feel that the deficiency payment on eggs might be made on a quarterly basis.
That is the position of the Liberal party.

I will tell my hon. friend the position of the Liberal party in a moment or two. We know their position in western Canada. We know the Liberal party is dead. We know they have not any agricultural policy. I can also quote what the hon. member for Essex East said when this program was brought into the house. He threw it aside and said it was nothing. He did not know what he was talking about. He made a big speech for an hour and a half-

Supply-Agriculture
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. gentleman permit a question?
If you will wait until I have finished my speech I will answer all the questions you wish to ask.
Thank you.

As I was saying, the initiation of the new program for hogs and eggs required a great deal of courage on the part of the former minister of agriculture. We in Alberta are particularly proud that he had the courage to introduce this kind of program, in spite of strong protests from some organized groups. We think, as he did, that after a year's trial certain changes might be made.
Then I would go on to one other subject under the stabilization act. I ask that the minister give further consideration, as he has in the past, to the whole question of the sheep industry, particularly in western Canada, under the rehabilitation scheme. In our area we are interested in this industry. We feel we could go a long way in developing a proper sheep industry there with a higher support price for lamb, with the continuation of the present support price through deficiency payments on wool, and the establishment of information and experimental stations, sheep flocks for crossbreeding, and other technical details to help our sheep farmers develop a strong sheep industry in that particular area.
In the last three years we have developed a good national policy for agriculture. Its main points are good. As I have said, some of them require the wrinkles ironed out. I am sure this will come as time goes by.
I wish to say a word with regard to acreage payments. The hon. member for Essex East says that the Liberal party policy is such and such. I know that out of the Liberal rally came the big idea that we should pay something like $300 on a unit quota. How well would this go over in my area? I will tell the hon. member and the committee several things with regard to acreage payments and permit books. In 1958, when this government made the first acreage payment, there were 1,800 new permits issued in my constituency. Why were these new permits issued? They were issued primarily because we have an area which is just now being developed agriculturally, and we do not have the delivery stations or the railway stations that some of the other areas in the prairies have.
We found that in 1958 the Canadian wheat board did not know anything about 25 per cent of the agricultural land in my constituency. As a matter of fact, over 50 per cent of the farmers in my area would have received absolutely nothing under the Liberal

party scheme or the C.C.F. scheme for deficiency payments. I am very proud to be able to say that most of them received payments under the acreage payments scheme.
However I do have a quarrel with some of the officers of the Canadian wheat board. I think this is another example of people who are working for the government thinking they have become so smart that they should take over the policies and legislation of the government. I wish to say with regard to the question of issuing permit books to the producers in my area the Canadian wheat board have at times, and are now, discriminating against the farmers of my region. This is not the result of a government decision; it is a decision made by some of the civil servants of the Canadian wheat board. I say this with adequate proof, and I wish to quote for the record the opinion of the solicitor to the Canadian wheat board at Winnipeg concerning who should be entitled to a permit book in any one year. I quote from a memorandum of Henry B. Monk, solicitor to the chief commissioner of the Canadian wheat board:
In the writer's view to be entitled to a permit book under the Canadian Wheat Board Act the applicant must first qualify as a person engaged in the production of grain or as a producer within the foregoing. At the time of his application in this respect I would not regard the fact that the applicant had all his land in summer fallow or seeded to forage crops or had no grain on hand as necessarily conclusive against the application. The question at issue in deciding each application for a permit book must be what is the bona fide purpose and object of the applicant's farming operations.
I wish to say that in 1958 the Canadian wheat board did not follow out the instructions of its solicitor. In 1960 and 1961 they have not followed the instructions of their solicitor in issuing permit books to some of the farmers in my area.
I went further and obtained from a lawyer who is well known to members of this house another legal opinion as to who should be entitled to permit books under the Canadian Wheat Board Act. This is the opinion he has given me;
I am of the opinion that the recent suggestion of the Board that farmers having only cultivated lands producing grain qualify for delivery permit books is not substantiated either by anything in the Wheat Board Act or in the wheat board regulations or in the western grain producers acreage payment regulations nor is it consistent with the interpretation placed on the act and on the regulations by the board itself in dealing with other farmers.
I would ask the minister to take this matter up with the Canadian wheat board because there has been discrimination in my area against farmers who had permit books in 1958-59 and who had permit books in 1960-61. They were refused a further permit book because it was said that they did not

have acreage under grain in 1959-60. In taking this position, the board was not carrying out its obligations as determined by its own solicitor and I would ask the minister to investigate this problem and correct the situation as soon as possible.
There has been some suggestion on occasion, particularly from government officials, that the region which I have the honour to represent is not a grain producing area. I wish to correct that impression. Only last year the world barley king at the Toronto Royal Winter Fair, Mr. George Lamb, came from the town of Cherhill. We have had numerous world wheat kings from the area of Wolf Creek, which is in the vicinity of the Rockies in western Alberta. We can and do grow grain in our area. I hope recognition that we do will be forthcoming, and that the farmers may be treated accordingly.
Now I wish to turn to the feed grain regulations about which we have heard a great deal in this house. We have seen the hon. member for Assiniboia get up and wave his hands. We do not know what the Liberals think about this-I doubt whether they have any thoughts about it at all. We have seen the hon. member for Assiniboia claim we are wrecking the wheat board. We are doing nothing of the kind. In my opinion the new regulations will strengthen the board. First of all, they will give the board a comprehensive idea of all the land under cultivation in western Canada, something which it did not have before. Again, a secondary feed industry is needed in western Canada to provide us with the necessary equipment so as properly to finish our product and increase its market value. This will provide a secondary industry in western Canada and correspondingly create more jobs in that area, something which the hon. member for Assiniboia seems unwilling to do.
Reverting for a few moments to this question of permit books, in the light of the experience with the wheat board I wish to suggest to the minister that we scrap the entire permit department of the board and set up in its place local authorities in the municipalities who would have the duty of issuing permits to the farmers in the area. In this way we might bring an end to the business of father and son, brother and brother, or husband and wife partnerships operated so as to secure two permit books. Let us get back to good democratic principles. Let us say to the farmers: we are going to set up boards in your area and these cases will be judged by your peers. These are the people who will say whether or not you are going to have a permit book. It seems to me this could be done by using the field crop men who are already at work
Supply-Agriculture
in western Canada, by using the district's agriculturists, by having representatives from the pools and the elevators and of the farmers themselves on these boards. It seems to me that a board composed of three such men could equitably distinguish between those who should receive permit books and those who should not. It would be far better done this way than by some civil servants in Winnipeg who have no knowledge of the land in question and who sometimes make arbitrary decisions one way or another. I hope the minister will at least give consideration to this view, because I think it would constitute a step forward in returning to the principles of democracy.
I wish to make some comments on one subject in connection with the experimental farm service. I want to ask the minister to set up an experimental farm on the muskeg we have in western Canada so that this land might, in time, produce the crops which it could produce after proper study and development. Right now we are importing into Canada, an agricultural country, crops worth in the neighbourhood of $650 million a year. This is a tremendous sum to spend on importing goods of this character into an agricultural country, though I realize that a portion of these imports is made up of fresh fruit and vegetables grown during the off season in some more southerly regions. On the other hand, there are a great many things which are imported into Canada which we could be growing ourselves and some of them, I believe, could be grown on the many millions of acres of muskeg we have in this country. I know the minister is interested in projects of this sort. I know he has paid a great deal of attention to conservation and that his work in connection with rural rehabilitation could mean a great deal for us in parts of northwest Alberta.
I wish to mention briefly the subject of butter and its support price. In addition, if I may be so bold, I should like to refer to reports with medical implications which have been rife in the lay press of late. I wish to say that as a country general practitioner I have in the past year conducted some very rough experimental work in my area on the cholesterol levels of the blood. I wish to take this opportunity of passing on to the committee and the public at large my findings in this respect. I agree with those renowned scientists who say that butter is a grade A food which we can eat and enjoy without regard for the bogey man of coronary thrombosis, for behind the threat of coronary thrombosis are a number of other factors besides the cholesterol level in the blood.
I think the greatest underlying factor is a lack of exercise. Canadians and the people

Supply-Agriculture
of the United States in general are victims of what we might call transportationitis which leads to their taking little physical exercise. This, rather than the overeating of fats, is probably the greatest cause of heart disease. Of course, I hasten to say that moderation in all things is a sound principle the application of which is essential for good health and this applies to the consumption of animal fats as it applies to other foods.
We certainly will not improve the general standard of health of Canadians by subscribing to every new fad diet that comes along. As a matter of fact, it can be shown there is a correlation between the amount of heart disease in the country and the number of automobiles and television sets to be found there. But this of course does not represent the entire answer.
I wish to suggest to the minister and the government that we commission the national research council, through its medical division, to undertake a further comprehensive study of the question of cholesterol in the blood and that the findings of this study be correlated with the research done in various other countries so that we may find a proper and reasonable answer to this problem.
Certainly there is no reason at all at the present time for Canadians not to eat butter. It is a complete fallacy that anything would be gained by substituting margarine for butter because the process of the hydrogenation of vegetable oil into margarine renders it a fat chemically equivalent to butter. I wish to place these brief points on the record because I feel, although there is no way of measuring the degree, the drop in domestic butter consumption has been caused to some extent by lay press reports concerning arteriosclerosis and heart disease resulting from the overeating of animal fats. I suggest this is not true and that there is no evidence to support this contention. I suggest, rather, that these diseases arise from complex factors, that these are complicated conditions in which a number of factors play a part, such as stress, inherited resistance and others. Again I ask the minister to suggest to the national research council that they undertake a study to correlate information pertaining to this important subject.
In concluding let me pay a general tribute to the Department of Agriculture and, in particular, to the veterinary medical branch for the excellent work they have done in Canada which has made Canada's veterinary medical health service one of the best in the world. Having had some previous experience with the department in this regard, I can assure the committee and the country that we

in Canada are fortunate in having such an effective group working under the able direction of the director general.
These are the comments I wished to place on the record. Again I invite the minister to investigate my complaints with regard to the issuing of permits through the Canadian wheat board. This is of particular importance to the farmers in the western portion of my constituency, who do not enjoy the privileges or the easy access to elevators and transportation that are enjoyed by the other farmers in western Canada.
If my friend the hon. member for Essex East has any questions I shall be very pleased to answer them.

Mr. Chairman, I simply want to ask the hon. member about the suggestion he has made with regard to the application of the principle of regionalization to the deficiency payments on hogs. Does the hon. member not recall that that proposal was made by me on behalf of the Liberal party at the last session of parliament? Is he not aware that our proposal is consistent with the recommendations made recently to the government by the federation of agriculture, and turned down by the government? We welcome the support of the hon. gentleman in this regard.

Finally I am able to welcome some reasonable support from the hon. member for Essex East who will recall that when speaking about this subject he said, "It is a good thing, but". Then, he proceeded to qualify his endorsement of the principle. I cannot quote the hon. member directly but it will be recalled that at that time the minister said he was eager to try the scheme for a year to see if it would average out properly, and if it did not the government would do something about it. All the farmers in my area accepted that. We now come to the government and say we do not think that national averaging was a good principle.
And we agree with you.

I am pleased that the hon. gentleman finally agrees with something that will be of benefit to the farmers. It is the first time the hon. member has ever done so.

Before dealing with the matter of agricultural research I would like to make a few general remarks.
In view of the importance of this branch, so vital to the welfare of all Canadians, I felt it would have been appropriate for the minister, in submitting his estimates, to make a comprehensive statement on the present

position of agriculture in this country, on the problems our farmers have to face today, and to explain the relation between the estimates he is asking us to vote and the plan which the government proposes to carry out to raise farm income.
In his speech, the minister stated that 21 per cent of Canadian farms bring less than $1,200 yearly income to their operators. While this is obviously a disturbing figure, I am still more concerned over the present status of family farm operators, many of whom are found not only in the province of Quebec but also in central Ontario, in the maritimes, and elsewhere.
Mr. Chairman, I am asking myself to what extent those sums of money we are asked to vote will improve the situation of our farmers. I listened carefully to the statement which the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) made on February 24 last, I have read and reread his report, because I wanted to take part in the discussion, as I did in 1958 and 1959.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I think that, after thoroughly considering the matter, the minister himself will admit that nothing in his speech holds out any very comforting prospects for our farmers. Yet the problems are there before us. They are serious by reason of their extent, and they are urgent. To talk of farming in Canada in 1961 is to talk of low and uncertain price levels, unstable and inadequate income, selling at a loss and surplus production. Those are, in general, the difficulties which our rural producers have to face.
No amount of speeches or statistical gimmicks can change any of the facts facing us in 1961. The answer to such conditions lies in over-all planning, in new and dynamic prospects. In other words, what is required is a national farm policy, in keeping with the needs of the moment.
If the government has any plan to offer, now is the time to do it. Until then, we are and shall be justified in saying that the government is not up to its task, is not assuming its responsibilities in the matter of agriculture, and that farmers in this country can rightfully say and repeat that they are not receiving their fair share of the national income.
Mr. Chairman, I listened with great care to the speeches of the hon. members for Drum-mond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger) and for Beauce (Mr. Racine), who very clearly explained to us the problems peculiar to Quebec,
Supply-Agriculture
as well as other matters of national scope with regard to the farming industry.
I hope the government will note the recommendations of those two hon. members and act upon them.
Mr. Chairman, I was quite amused when the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), at the beginning of his remarks, compared the speech made by the Minister of Agriculture and those made under the former government by the Hon. Mr. Gardiner. This provides me with an opportunity to recall the legendary figure of Mr. Gardiner and the debt of gratitude which Canadian farmers owe him. Let me say, therefore, to the hon. member who spoke before me and who referred to a national policy, that if he and his colleagues in the government are really interested in working out a policy, I heartily suggest that they consult the official record of debates under the former administration. They will see how vigorously and boldly Mr. Gardiner set out to apply an agricultural policy in this country, at a time when the major problem facing him was a problem of production. When Mr. Gardiner left the administration, he could take pride in the fact that in the matter of production, Canada's farmers were in the position he had dreamed for them, that is to say they were at that time the greatest wheat producers in the world.
Mr. Chairman, since the years 1956-57, great changes have occurred. It is unfortunate that this government has remained in a static position, because technology and scientific research have been transforming not only industry but also agricultural operations in Canada. Even more serious, such changes have also occurred in other countries of the world, so that today countries which at the time were our customers have now become our competitors. If as soon as it took over the country's administration this government had taken note of those structural changes, the yield of our farms would be much higher than it is now.
This view was expressed just recently not only by specialists and experts but also by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture in the brief it submitted to the government on March 1 last. This brief not only reflects our present agricultural problems but offers to the government various practical solutions which could not be safely ignored.
The Montreal Gazette, in an editorial which appeared on March 2 last, reported on some

Supply-Agriculture
comments with regard to this brief from the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and mentioned the fourteen suggestions put forward in this brief to the government. I quote: (Text):
In the annual brief which it submitted to Prime
Minister Diefenbaker and other federal cabinet ministers for the calendar year 1961, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture laid it right on the line.
The federation was downright disturbed by a tendency which it saw developing. And it didn't hesitate to speak out.
The federation, as it turned out, came well armed with constructive proposals.
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, this brief raises a very important question, one which I consider vital and which establishes something that we, in the official opposition, have been preaching for years, that is to say the interdependence of farm policy and business policy. May I therefore be allowed to read very slowly a few lines from page 5 of the brief submitted by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture:
(Text):
Trade In agricultural products is, of course, but one aspect of general trade, and is vitally affected by general trade policies. It was the opinion of the delegate body that there are at present heavy pressures from secondary industry for an increased degree of protection, and it would view with alarm any trend in this direction in Canada. There are of course fundamental issues and philosophies of economic policy involved here. As a surplus producer of agricultural products Canada has a great and fundamental stake in expanding trade. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture believes that the long-run interests of Canada lie in its development as a modern industrial trading nation, rather than a nation with the pattern of its industrial development shaped by a policy of increasing protection for Canadian manufacturing industry.
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, there is obviously no point in producing, or in improving production methods if, on the other hand, the government, by its shortsighted commercial policy, does not at the same time take steps to promote the marketing of our products throughout the world.
I hope the government will reconsider its position in trade matters, because in a country like ours with its surplus problems, the only possible solution, the only plausible one, is a bold and dynamic policy of expanded trade. To that end, hon. members will recall that the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Pearson) missed no opportunity to express that view. In fact, at the Liberal rally, last January, one promptly adopted resolution advocated that policy of economic expansion, which would save our farm producers from their present predicament.
Mr. Chairman, the brief of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture puts great emphasis

on research. Allow me to read, in this connection, a few lines from page 17 of the brief: (Text):
In a different field, we would bring to your attention that we believe, in view of the need for developing markets for farm products to an absolute maximum, that there should be stepped up programs by the national research council aimed at developing new and better utilization of farm products. Investigation into the use of wheat in food forms other than bread has been specifically mentioned as an area of research needing attention.
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, in 1958 and 1959, I drew the attention of the minister of agriculture who today is Minister of National Defence to that matter. And, according to page 2401 of Hansard of 1959, I said this:
I wish to bring to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) a very important point. I feel that if we are to improve the efficiency of agriculture in this country, in the west as well as in the eastern and central parts of this country, we should at once adjust our research procedure. Let us set up a new co-ordination of existing services and give a new, bold and forward looking impulse to these research services-
Mr. Chairman, I understand that since January 1 last the minister has proceeded to a diversion of technical and research services with regard to marketing under the Canadian wheat board. I shall say right away that this is a step in the right direction. It is unfortunate that his predecessor, who is now Minister of National Defence, did not think it advisable to start setting up such a service two or three years ago.
We have of course in our service efficient experts and the most up-to-date material facilities with regard to research; but, if I am not mistaken, about 98 per cent of our research is still focused on production or the improvement of production methods.
I submit that it is absolutely necessary to underline the economic aspect. We should apply to agriculture the same methods which have been so successful in industry. How can production costs be reduced, how can the quality of our products be raised, and how can they be made marketable abroad? That is the whole Canadian farm problem which must be considered anew in the light of modern scientific information.
According to page 2407 of Hansard, the minister had a word to say on the matter on February 24, 1961. I quote:
Another point I should like to mention in this connection is that it is now very obvious that there are other things for which wheat can be utilized besides the traditional products, bread. It is no secret that thousands of years ago wheat and barley were used as a staple diet not in the form of bread. In many countries of the world where the tendency to turn to the use of the

new product, bread, is slow, it might be possible for us to sell wheat ready for human consumption closer to the natural form.
Mr. Chairman, with regard to this question of bread, I would like to make two remarks. First of all, I shall repeat a question recently asked by the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Macnaughton) who inquired from experts:
How can it be that we have, in this country, the best wheat and perhaps the worst bread in the world?
I leave it to the experts to comment upon it. My second remark is consequential to what I just said. I note in the report of the standing committee on agriculture and colonization, volume 10, page 138, that bread consumption in Canada per head is falling off in an alarming way.
The problem was submitted to experts and I am wondering whether the national research council would not have here a field to explore with a view to improving the quality of the bread we eat and, second, to finding the reasons why bread consumption has decreased in Canada, while our population is constantly on the increase.
In connection with those remarks, I would also like to mention my personal views with regard to the matter of research.
We know that in several other countries of the world, such as southern Asia-I refer particularly to India and China-the staple food is rice. Those countries, however, are chronically famished, while we have surpluses.
I wonder, Mr. Chairman, whether our research division could not step up its work so that we might offer those countries some of our surplus products in a form that they could eat and assimilate.
I think, Mr. Chairman, that the research council should also look into the most important matter of family farms.
In the minister's own statement as recorded on page 2405 of Hansard, we were informed that from year to year, the number of our farmers declined by about 10,000 a year. I quote the figures he gave. In 1958, there were
555,000	farmers; in 1959, 546,000 and in 1960, 536,000. I say, Mr. Chairman, that these statistics are alarming. All the more so because the bulk of these figures consists of family farms. This, I think, involves the most stable element of our population.
I think we have a duty to consider immediately the reasons why, from year to
Supply-Agriculture
year, there is a decline in the number of farms, and particularly family farms, in Canada. I refer not only to the province of Quebec but also to other provinces.
I think this problem must be considered in our research effort. In the last analysis, it is a matter of determining what should be the exact structure or the mould of a family farm. Through such a study, a means might be found to make such farms economically sound and profitable.
And to show the economic benefits which can accrue from agricultural research, I was reading a few days ago in a Montreal newspaper that a manufacturer whose industry depends on imported vegetable oils-I think it refers to Mr. Pascale Gattuso-had decided to conduct experiments in Manitoba with this fodder plant called rapeseed, and from which vegetable oil is extracted. Well, through the initiative of a businessman, we now have in Manitoba a co-operative producing vegetable oil. I wonder why this initiative was taken by one of our businessmen rather than by our research experts.
On how many items is our trade dependent on imports? How many of those items could we produce ourselves? I have mentioned this example just to show the full importance of the research division.
Mr. Chairman, it is through scientific research that we have been able to increase production and sales, and raise the yield of our plants, our land and our stocks. We have doubled and even tripled the yield. It does seem that it is also through scientific research that we can substantially reduce our surpluses.
The time has come to throw into this struggle a larger portion of our financial resources.
Mr. Chairman, I understand that next fall a conference will be held in Montreal on "Resources and our future", all the provinces, as well as the Department of Agriculture and the federal government, will be represented.
I should like to quote from this booklet which has been submitted to us, a paragraph which shows the approach to be taken at this conference, and I quote:
Great stress will be laid on the vast problem of land use for agricultural purposes. It is known how difficult it is for domestic farms in the prairies to survive as such, and how quickly Ontario's farm lands become unproductive (at the rate of a million acres every four or five years); it is known at what rate the orchards in the Ontario peninsula and the farms along the south shore of the St. Lawrence, towards Montreal, are

Supply-Agriculture
being taken over as industrial sites. In less than ten years, the agricultural situation has changed to such an extent that it can no longer be studied except on a national basis.
So, Mr. Chairman, I do hope that at that conference, a practical scheme will be worked out.
To that end, I should like to put forward a suggestion. I was saying a moment ago that as a result of the change in production techniques and of the fact that certain countries which were formerly our customers are now our competitors, what we need today in the agricultural field is to find out where we stand and work out a program.
I recognize at the outset that this is no easy task. Why? Canada will always have two major difficulties to overcome ir, the agricultural field. In the first place, we have an extremely vast territory; I think we have have the greatest area of tillable land in the world. The second problem is that the territory being heterogeneous, our land use is completely different from one point to another.
In view of those difficulties and of those important problems, and in view of the fact that we must necessarily take an inventory before drawing up a practical program on a national basis-a program which would be practical not only for the west or for central Canada but also for the east and for the maritime, in other words a truly national program, I wonder whether it would not be desirable to set up within the department a joint advisory council, as it was suggested at our last convention, a council in which every part of Canada would be represented. Those experts would have no other administrative duty than to study, comment, inform and suggest to the government what, to their mind, would be the most practical thing to do, in the various areas they represent.
The department would also have available some qualified and representative men from all parts of this country, who would be familiar with the special problems of those districts. Moreover, should a problem arise in any part of the country, then the minister could have those experts make inquiries on the spot.
I think the establishment of such a board would be to the benefit of the government and certainly in the best interest of the whole country.
Mr. Chairman, those are my suggestions. I hope that the minister will take them into consideration. Before closing my remarks, may I draw the attention of my hon. friends from the Conservative party, and more particularly of

those who represent the rural and agricultural districts, to the fact that, in 1958 they received a token of trust, such as no government ever received before. In 1958, they obtained-
That will happen again in 1962.
-this vote of confidence by making promises. Now I would point out that, at this time, those promises have not been kept.
Which ones?

I shall tell my hon. friends that time is pressing them, because, very soon, their political future will be their past and they shall have to face those who have sent them here.

I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but his time has expired.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, it is a pleasure to take the floor after the farmer-lawyer from Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets). My task will be that much easier, since his knowledge of agriculture seems to be limited. However, I would not like to be considered as an expert myself in agriculture. Be that as it may, it seems to me my hon. friend from Maisonneuve-Rosemont could have learned his lesson better, before lecturing Conservative members who none the less received, as he did say, a testimony of invaluable confidence on the part of the people, especially on the part of farmers.
It is true, Mr. Chairman, that the present Conservative government has received unlimited confidence from the agricultural class, because during the 21 years they were in power, the Liberal government failed dismally to live up to the task. Mr. Chairman, I should like to recall to the house some of the measures we have taken since we have been in power.
Mr. Chairman, may I first be allowed to remind the house that one of the first measures taken by the Conservative government after having been elected, after having obtained the confidence of the people, as the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets) said a moment ago, was to put at the disposal of farmers $250 million as a revolving fund to stabilize the prices of farm products.
I should like also to remind all members that in 1959 the Conservative government granted, in subsidies to dairy products, the

sum of $4,750,000. In 1960, that is from May to December, those subsides reached the amount of $3,750,000.
Furthermore, in 1960, the Conservative government paid $208,394.92 in support prices on eggs.
We all know that the Canadian Farm Loan Act has been improved substantially under the present Conservative administration.
Under our Liberal friends farmers could only borrow $15,000, while under the present Conservative administration they may borrow up to $20,000, since such loans are calculated now on the basis of 75 per cent of the value of the farm, while under the Liberal administration it was on the basis of only 65 per cent.
The Farm Improvement Loans Act was amended by the Conservative government and the amount of the loan was increased from $5,000 to $7,000.
Mr. Chairman, all those improvements have been made to the great resentment of our Liberal friends, whose whining we are hearing today and who were not able, during the 21 years they were in power, to understand the agricultural class.
Mr. Chairman, I should like all Canadian farmers to remember those things so that when the time comes for another general election they may not be fooled by our Liberal friends, who after a delay of 21 years now claim to be the friends of farmers.
Mr. Chairman, at the time of the Liberal administration the subsidy paid under the Animal Contagious Diseases Act was $100 per purebred animal slaughtered; the Conservative government increased that subsidy to $140 per animal. The sum of $40 which was paid for each half-bred animal slaughtered has been increased to $70.
Mr. Chairman, at this stage of my remarks, I should like to take a few minutes to inform the house of what the Conservative party policy has meant for the constituency I have the honour to represent.
Thanks to the measures introduced by the present Conservative government, thanks to the initiative of the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) and of his predecessor, the present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Harkness), the citizens of my constituency received in 1959 the sum of $221,523.04 in subsidies on dairy products; those subsidies reached $295,364 in 1960.
As for sugar beets, farmers of my constituency received in subsidies the sum of
Supply-Agriculture
$41,390.70, while in 1960 the 65,000 tons of sugar beets produced in our area brought to farmers of my constituency the sum of $74,015. I would suggest to the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) to take good note of those figures.
Mr. Chairman, I might inform the house that through the beneficial legislation proposed by the Minister of Agriculture in the present government, a farmer of my riding has received an amount of $1,300, a thing that never happened under the previous Liberal government. In addition, he benefited from other grants under legislation passed by the Conservative government.
Mr. Chairman, I realize that our Liberal friends, especially the members for Maison-neuve-Rosemont and for Essex East, both of them lawyers, now wish to get closer to the farm people. But as in the story of the hare and the tortoise, it is too late to start when the opponent is already at the winning post.
Gentlemen of the Liberal party, you may well grieve. You have every reason to be sorry, because you have had your chance to show what you could do for the farm people. As for us, even though we came later, we knew how to take advantage of the situation and we gave to the farm people what they were entitled to expect from a truly Canadian government, devoted to all Canadians and not only to the Liberals.
Gentlemen of the Liberal party, you may give up that opportunity as lost, but we, of the Conservative party, are forging ahead, and we shall go from one achievement to the other, to the satisfaction of our constituents, people who are only waiting for the chance to return us to office with an even greater majority.
Mr. Chairman, may I put a question to the hon. member for St. Hyacin-the-Bagot?
Certainly. In view of your ignorance, I can answer all your questions.
Mr. Chairman, I wish the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot would tell me when the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) will keep his promise about a price support on pulpwood?

Mr. Chairman, let me first of all remind the house that the present premier of Quebec, who for some months travelled all over the province, promising to do and

Supply-Agriculture
give all sorts of things certainly has a duty to fulfil in that respect. However, the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska may rest assured that as long as the Minister of Agriculture and the Conservative party have a responsibility in the matter the party will certainly honour its obligations, contrary to what happened under the administration of those for whom he cares much.
(Text):

Whenever the agriculture estimates are under discussion I see in my mind's eye the hon. member for Assiniboia up to his ears in grain. I almost hear the lowing of cattle waiting to be fed and I can smell bales of new mown hay.
While I was listening to the doxology to Conservatism and the hymn of thanksgiving for Conservative policies a moment or two ago, I could not help but remember reading some reports and statistics recently. Surely, while the hon. gentleman was performing this eulogy and protecting the flanks of the Minister of Agriculture he must have remembered that the province of Quebec has had a form of Conservative government for 16 years.
It did very well for the province, too.
And the net income per farmer for Quebec is one of the lowest in Canada.
Because the earlier Liberal regime did not accept its responsibility.
Oh.

Now, I want to express my appreciation for the courtesy with which the Minister of Agriculture has attended to any of my complaints, that is, to individual complaints, not complaints relating to the whole farming industry. I have found the hon. gentleman courteous and co-operative in that respect and I appreciate it. I suppose it would be fair to say that the Minister of Agriculture is the roving ambassador for the government. From his remarks when the discussion of these estimates began, there appears no doubt that while he has not been able to present substantial solutions to many of the problems now facing agriculture he is finding out what the problems of the farmer are. I also wish to express my appreciation of the good work of the senior staff and the field men of the department. We must not forget, when we discuss these estimates in the relative comfort of this chamber-that is, the comfort of all of us except the minister-that the field staff do a lot of slogging 
day by day. It is not very glamorous work; it does not reach the newspapers, and to many people it is unknown. However, the department has some excellent field staff officers. I have known many of them for a goodly number of years, and I want to express the appreciation of this group for the work they are doing.
I do not intend to speak at length at this stage of the discussion because I shall have various things to say on the particular items as they arise, but I do want to speak briefly on one or two matters. I think one of the first things to be done is to get the public to recognize the importance of agriculture to the Canadian economy and to the country. There is a tendency to underestimate the importance of agriculture because, shall I say, of the dynamism of the growth of industry and things of that sort.
I notice that the hon. member for Essex East is listening intently, and I want to say this in connection with that hon. member. The member for Essex East is not a farmer but I know from lengthy discussions with him that he is a student of farmers' problems and needs, and that is what is required at this time. There has to be a greater recognition on the part of the people of Canada as a whole of the importance of agriculture, and this is lacking in many quarters. There is a tendency to underestimate it and in some cases almost to jeer at the maintenance of the economic family farm and agriculture of that type.
I think there a responsibility falls on the Department of Agriculture, as well as on the provincial departments and the farm organizations, to improve their public relations so as to inform the remainder of the population of the importance of the agricultural sector of the economy. In this connection, I wish briefly to read from a magazine called "Canadian Commentator" which often contains some very informative articles. The issue of June, 1960 to which I am referring contains an article by Mr. George R. McLaughlin on the Canadian farmer which I think puts the question very well indeed. I quote briefly from this article:
I have been concerned these last few years about the misunderstanding which exists in the minds of non-farmers with regard to the economic position of farm people in this land of plenty. This misunderstanding has grown for quite obvious reasons, and there seems little indication that agriculture's public relations, if there is such a thing, has done much to correct the situation.
It goes on to say:
Not many people realize that the farmers of Canada represent a consumer's market of some $2.8 billion a year, about $1.7 billion of which is spent for the goods and services required in the production of food, and another $1.1 billion

for the requirements of family living, such as radios and cosmetics, children's toys and lawn mowers, coffee and canned goods, skates and cameras, furniture and overcoats, and all the hundreds of other goods and services required by any family, urban or rural. In the United States it has been said that the farmer as a consumer of goods and services is worth two and a half times as much as any other individual consumer in the country. I see no reason why the same comparison should not be used in Canada.
I think that is very well put indeed. There should be a public relations job done to inform the people of the importance of agriculture not only to the farmer but to the rest of the economy.
I could not help noticing, in the quotation I read, a reference to the purchase of cosmetics. What a change there has been in the world in which we live. I remember 50 years ago talking to a farmer who had to drive many miles along a mountain trail to get his groceries. He did not use cosmetics, nor did his wife. He got into the habit of putting a rooster into the crate to accompany him on his journey so that he would not be lonely. What a difference in the way things are done today. I have lived in the same circumstances, and I am proud of it.
It is only fitting when speaking on the estimates of this department to make some reference to the fact that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture has celebrated its twenty fifth anniversary. I was very closely associated with the British Columbia federation of agriculture and on that account I realize what good work the organization has done throughout the years for the Canadian farmer. In saying this, I fully recognize the excellent work which has been done by other organizations, such as the farmers' union and those organizations connected with particular branches of the industry. In the early days our first president was the Hon. E. D. Barrow, former Liberal minister of agriculture of British Columbia and a great personal friend of mine.
Where did he live?

Chilliwack. He was a practical farmer who spent many years of his life working for his fellow farmers in British Columbia. I think we should remember these things. There was also Mr. Charles Hayden, the first secretary-treasurer, who lived in Vernon. Under his guidance the work of the organization was greatly developed. At the present time the British Columbia federation of agriculture has a membership of between
16,000	and 17,000 which shows how important the agriculture industry is in British Columbia when we relate it to other industries in the province.
Supply-Agriculture
I am pleased to see the hon. member for Cariboo has his hearing aid on and is listening to me, determined not to miss a single one of my words of wisdom.
Before taking my seat, I want to refer to some of the matters brought to the attention of the government by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. I will avoid repetition and mention only those points that are important to the farmers I represent and farmers generally across the country.
In their brief, the federation indicate great interest in marketing farm products in commercial markets overseas and also in the development of the world food pool under the United Nations as well as other agencies for the proper use of our surpluses. In their representations they presented a resolution to the government in these words:
1.	Receive from nations having the ability to do so, undertakings to contribute to an internationally conducted program of food distribution to areas of need. Such contributions could take the form of commitments to supply food, or could take the form of funds, or necessary services for transporting food contributions to needy countries.
2.	Receive and appraise information on food needs, and, on the basis of such information and the requests of participating nations, carry out the equitable distribution of the food supplies made available.
3.	Co-ordinate and advise on the orderly conduct of non-commercial food distribution in its broadest implications. The aim of such consultation and co-ordination should be to give direction and purpose, through the United Nations, to all programs and activities contributing to the goal of an international food program.
To indicate what farmers are thinking I wish to quote a statement made by the president of the British Columbia federation of agriculture:
H. D. Arnold of Duncan, president of the B.C. federation of agriculture, told the B.C. fruit growers association that Canada could do more for the world by helping backward nations in peaceful development than it could possibly achieve by its own armament.
He urged all sections of agriculture to press this viewpoint.
Mr. Arnold agreed that arms expenditure should be slashed-but instead of cutting taxes with the money so saved, he would spend it building up and developing backward countries.
He suggested Canada should select one or two countries and concentrate on them, or contribute to a master international fund for the same purpose.
"From a propaganda viewpoint alone," he said, "the other countries would not stand by and let us do it on our own."
"A tractor or a plow sent to Nigeria, for instance, would do more for world peace than providing another tank for our armed forces; better a fruit ladder to Nigeria than an aircraft.
That is a growing sentiment among farmers and I was pleased to see that this gentleman thinks along lines similar to those of hon. members of this group.
I shall mention one or two other matters of particular importance to the people in my

Supply-Agriculture
district. In addition to supplying food overseas, all sections of the British Columbia Federation of Agriculture are concerned about the cost of taxation of the land for educational purposes. This reference is found at page 7 of the brief of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, and I will quote briefly from it because it concerns British Columbia farmers who believe that there must be some change in taxation, in view of the increased costs of hospitals and education, if the economic family farm is to continue to exist. The brief reads:
One subject which we would mention only briefly-although it is a matter of very great importance-is that of education costs. It is becoming more and more widely recognized that as the importance and the cost of education increases that two things are necessary: first that a high standard of education and educational opportunity should be assured for every Canadian child; second, that the real property tax imposed by the local school district is becoming increasingly inadequate and inequitable as a basis for meeting education costs. This inadequacy and inequity does not concern the farmer alone, but as a heavy investor in land in relation to his income the farmer tends to feel the situation much more keenly.
They propose that this matter must receive the attention of the government.
The federation also deals with the question of transportation, with which I shall not deal at length. They deal, too, with the question of land and water use and rural development. This is the subject of a resolution recently brought forward by the Minister of Agriculture, which I hope will come forward again in the near future.

Will the hon. member permit me to point out that at the bottom of page 10 of the brief, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture expresses the hope that the legislation on that subject introduced by the minister by way of resolution will be passed at this session of parliament and not postponed as the minister proposes.
I am glad that the hon. member for Essex East, with his usual attention to detail in these matters, has reminded me of this important part of the representation.
Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the hon. member who has the floor would mind telling the committee from what he and the other professional farmer who spoke are quoting?

I am surprised that the hon. member is ignorant of what has happened in Ottawa in recent weeks and months. I am reading from a presentation of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture to the Prime Minister of Canada and members of the cabinet on February 28, 1961. Incidentally, that is my birthday and a very important event. I was

born in London but only because my mother was visiting there that day. No doubt the hon. member has received a copy of this brief.

Mr. Chairman, I thank the hon. member. I certainly have a copy of the brief but I attend the meetings of these organizations and rarely read briefs. I must congratulate the hon. gentleman on celebrating his eightieth birthday.

The federation in its brief deals with land and water use and rural development and expresses the hope that the legislation will be passed this session, as the hon. member for Essex East so kindly reminded me.
There is another subject in which I am interested because of its increasing importance. I shall deal with it and one or two other matters only briefly. I dealt with research at some length on the minister's estimates last year and if anyone wishes to be well-informed as to the needs of agriculture in respect of research I suggest he look up the speech I made last year on item No. 1 of the minister's estimates.
The federation is still interested in medical health insurance. The recommendation in the brief on this point reads:
We do think no time should be lost in moving forward in the study of ways and means of aiding the provinces in the establishment of provincial medical health insurance plans.
This subject does not come directly under the Minister of Agriculture but the quotation shows that farmers are interested not only in their own problems but in problems of national scope and importance.
The federation also deals with unemployment insurance for farm workers. In this respect, I urge the government to act as soon as possible to institute a plan for unemployment insurance coverage for farm workers, either on voluntary or on a suitable selective basis.
It has frequently been said that farmers operate under severe circumstances. They may not want to work in industries or occupations covered by unemployment insurance. In conditions of full employment, nine times out of 10 an individual given a choice between working on a farm or accepting a position in industry will accept an industrial position. I urge the Minister of Agriculture to use his influence with the Minister of Labour to again stress the importance to the farmers of Canada of this subject.
I believe it was the British Columbia Federation of Agriculture which first brought forward a request with respect to land expropriation and easement, which subjects are also dealt with in the brief of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. We in British Columbia suffer from iniquitous laws in

respect to the expropriation of property for utilities, whether publicly or privately owned. There is absolutely no respect at all for the rights of the farmers or the land owners under the present legislation. Numerous instances have been brought to my attention of farmers whose timber had been cut down without any prior arrangements being made, of surveys being made, of fields being crossed, and things of that sort. This has created such concern that the British Columbia federation of agriculture has given the problem a great deal of study and has employed legal counsel. A good number of my constituents are concerned because, as the committee knows, the Minister of Justice has a plan under which 2,000 of them will be drowned in the near future if he has his way. They are all working together as a unit with the British Columbia federation of agriculture to try to protect their interests because, as I said before, the laws of British Columbia do not offer the proper protection. We are told that farmers are all for free, private ownership. Why, the government is destroying private enterprise, legitimate free enterprise and the small scale industry of farming right and left. Whenever the rights of the ordinary farmer come in conflict with the big corporations they go over the small farmer like a steamroller.
I should like to read a paragraph from page 18 of the brief of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture:
Land expropriation and easement.
The Railway Act provides that proceedings for drainage works arising out of the location of railways may be taken either under provincial law or under the provisions of the Railway Act. at the option of the land owner. It seems to us that this is a very reasonable principle in relation to problems of compensation and expropriation. We think this option principle should be extended to include all utilities operating under federal charter, and also to apply to proceedings not only for drainage works, but to proceedings for compensation and works connected with expropriation and easements generally.
I think it is the responsibility of the federal Minister of Agriculture, at the dominion-provincial agricultural conferences which are held annually, to work in co-operation with the ministers of agriculture of the provinces to provide some federal and provincial legislation which will protect the rights of Canadian citizens against vested interests and those who, up to date, have had the economic power to do what they like.
The federation commends the government's decision to hold an inquiry into farm machinery prices. We are glad that matter has been referred to a committee. I am also very pleased to see that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture has passed a resolution with respect to nuclear weapons, as follows:
Supply-Agriculture
Resolved that Canada should provide leadership in a plan to control the spread ol nuclear weapons by promoting an agreement of all nations that they will not test, manufacture, or possess any nuclear devices for warfare, and Further resolved that Canada should encourage that this agreement be under the jurisdiction of the United Nations.
I hope the minister will draw this resolution to the particular attention of the Secretary of State for External Affairs because I am sure that when he deals with the Minister of National Defence he will welcome the additional support he is receiving from the Canadian Federation of Agriculture.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture reiterates its strong support of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I have mentioned briefly the majority of the questions which the Canadian federation brought to the attention of the cabinet. I do urge that the minister give these serious consideration as representing the views of a very responsible segment of our economy, upon which a great deal depends in Canada, and for the welfare of which we should recognize our responsibility on all occasions.
I shall have a few things to say when we discuss the various items.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words on the agricultural estimates, since Waterloo county is a farming district equal to most counties in Ontario.
Although the growing of wheat, oats, corn and turnips is predominant, this county is well known for producing outstanding livestock and has on various occasions won prizes at the Canadian National Exhibition in Toronto as well as at other well known places.
The Waterloo county federation of agriculture was formed in 1944 and, along with junior farmers, has assisted the whole agricultural economy. The Waterloo county farmers have contributed much to the welfare of farming and the Mennonites, long established here, have carried on this work in a successful way.
Perhaps one of the problems is the lack of help on these farms, as many of the young people are entering other fields of activity. Last year a farmer friend of mine was unable to secure help. This was finally supplied when a Negro working in our district, being an agriculturalist, carried on the duties to the utmost satisfaction of his employer.
On a previous occasion the hon. member for Halton and I mentioned in the house the limited facilities which were available for hog testing programs at Waterloo, Ontario. In 1938, a 48-pen piggery was opened in Waterloo. The building program for the advanced registry station was resumed after the second world war and in 1948 a 60-pen

Supply-Agriculture
piggery was constructed at the Waterloo station. In 1959 the capacity of this station was 112 pens. Yet, the capacity of this station appears to be inadequate, as a number of entries have had to be turned away from time to time owing to the lack of sufficient facilities. While there has been some unused space in recent months, I should like to suggest to the government and the minister that they consider in detail the problem of more room. Mr. Ken Cappindale deserves a great deal of credit for his splendid work here. This station has played a prominent part in the breeding and selection of better hogs, and it must be increased in size if it is to continue to fulfil this objective.
The 4-H clubs have increased greatly, and I understand that today we have well over
77,000	boys and girls in this movement. They learn good practices at an age when they have no time to learn bad ones. They are a real credit to the agricultural set-up of our country, and their contributions are outstanding.
Elmira is the egg and chicken capital of Ontario. I understand that the largest broiler breeding farm in Ontario is located five miles from my home and operated by the Selling hatchery. The output last year was 2,500,000 chicks. In addition, three other major chick hatcheries are located in our area. They are the Reliable, the Bonny Chick and the Produce. It may be interesting to know that Mr. Seiling of the Seiling hatchery developed his own incubator and holds a patent on it. He has been in the business over 40 years. A few years ago the hatchery discontinued hatching laying chicks and now concentrates on the broiler market. Broilers are hatched the year round.
In my travels across Canada, especially across Ontario, I have been deeply impressed with the value of fall fairs in our villages, towns and cities. After all, they are the show windows of agriculture in our country. Displays of baking, dairy and good food products, crafts and art exhibits, along with a showing of cattle, hogs, horses and so on have provided a great deal of interest in many communities. Horse racing, of course, is always popular, as the hon. member for Victoria, Ontario, well knows.
In my own town of Elmira we held our 106th annual fall fair last year over the Labour day week end, at which time the attendance was 22,000 people drawn from a wide area.
In order to provide better facilities for our patrons the Elmira and Woolwich agricultural society are building a new grandstand to seat well over 1,000 people. It is interesting to know that all the directors of this society are farmers, or those having business dealings with them or a background of rural life. Their [Mr. Weichel.l
efforts have provided this fair with real possibilities for the future. Our memorial arena built on land owned by this society has seating accommodation for 1,500 people and many of the exhibits are shown in this building. As mentioned before, a new steel and cement block grandstand and exhibition building is being erected this year. Better facilities will be provided for the comfort of the people and also for the junior farmers and 4-H clubs which are all important in today's rural relationships. I hope that financial assistance will be available for this worthy project. In closing, may I commend the minister and his department for their efforts to bring about better conditions in agriculture.

Mr. Chairman, I listened very carefully to the remarks of the hon. member for Jasper-Edson and the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot. I cannot reply to the remarks made by the member from western Canada because I am not a farmer. I am an agriculturalist. So that there may be no mistake about the distinction between the two, may I say that a farmer is a man who makes his money in the country and spends it in the city while an agriculturalist is a man who makes his money in the city and spends it in the country.
The hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot spoke very glowingly of his constituency. I only wish I could speak as glowingly of mine because not since the hungry 30's have we had anything like the unemployment that we have in Renfrew North at the present time. The hon. member referred to the Farm Credit Corporation. May I say to him that he has very little cause to be worried for no organization of the government has done a better job, thanks to the personnel largely secured from the Veterans' Land Act administration, than the Farm Credit Corporation is doing at the present time. We have great hopes that the efficiency which was so evident in the administration of the Veterans' Land Act will be continued under the Farm Credit Corporation.
The hon. member for Jasper-Edson dealt with problems facing the farmers of western Canada. With that I have no quarrel, but not one word was spoken tonight, other than by the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot, with regard to eastern farmers. I am interested in having the question of the differences between the viewpoints of western farmers and eastern farmers aired in the standing committee on agriculture which is now sitting, and I would therefore ask the Minister of Agriculture to refer to that committee the problem of feedstuffs which is a sore spot in the economy of eastern Canadian farmers. I think this matter should

be referred to the committee so that we will be allowed to call witnesses both from the west and the east in order to see if we can solve this problem which is a serious one, particularly to the feed manufacturers and farmers of Ontario and Quebec.
Sometimes I really worry about the situation as far as eastern and western Canada are concerned. I once heard the remark made that if the North American continent had been divided at the Mississippi river conditions east and west of that line would probably be better than they are today. I do not want to suggest that we should have a minister of agriculture for western Canada and one for eastern Canada but nevertheless, having regard to the situation that exists in this part of the country, in my opinion this might be a brilliant idea.

That was three years ago and nothing has been done yet. I presume that these statements by the Prime Minister were not made for the purpose of gaining votes but I am afraid that is exactly what the tobacco growers have accused him of doing.
In 1953 the present Minister of Finance stated that in his opinion the tax on cigarettes and tobacco was too high and that if there was smuggling at the United States border it was largely due to the actions of the Liberal government in imposing sky-high excise taxes. What action did the Minister of Finance take when his government took over? He increased the excise tax on a package of cigarettes by two cents. The increase in the sales in 1959 was only 3.8 per cent, compared with an increasee of 7.5 per cent in the previous year.
The general value of flue-cured tobacco far exceeds the value of any other agricultural commodity. There are approximately 4,500 qualified farms in Ontario growing tobacco in 16 counties. The estimated capital investment in these farms is $300 million or an average of between $65,000 to $70,000 per farm. The farm buildings and equipment required to cultivate flue-cured tobacco is upwards of $40,000, depending on the size of the unit. Salaries and wages of the tobacco industry amount to over $30 million and the number of employees is over 10,000. There are over 50 tobacco products establishments in Canada.
When we examine the production figures we find that the total yield of all types of tobacco products from 1949 to 1959 was 1,600 million pounds and the excise tax and duty on cigarettes alone totalled $1,960 million. In 1958 the Conservative member for Norfolk, who is himself a substantial tobacco grower, urged the government to reduce the excise tax on cigarettes. A reduction in the taxes on cigarettes has been proved to be advantageous to the government because the reduced tax results in higher sales and yields a higher tax level. The accuracy of this statement was proven in 1952-53 when the minister of finance at that time, Mr. Abbott, cut the tax by two cents a pound and the revenue then increased by $7,800,000. I must say that Mr. Abbott raised the tax by two cents a pound the previous year but realized his mistake in so doing.
It has been pointed out to the government that if Canadian cigarettes could be made longer, without this additional cost of two cents per package, there exists the probability of a greatly increased export trade in Canadian cigarettes. It is obvious that it is highly advantageous to increase our export trade.

The forecast for next week subject to change is as follows: Monday and Tuesday a supply motion; Wednesday, interim supply and if concluded, supplementary estimates.
